title: Comparative effects of motor-control interventions on neuromuscular and biomechanical outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A systematic review and network meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neuromuscular-control and biomechanical deficits may persist after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). Comparative motor-control effects remain uncertain.
OBJECTIVES: To compare motor-control interventions after ACLR.
DESIGN: Systematic review and network meta-analysis.
METHOD: Seven databases were searched to 12 May 2026. Usual rehabilitation comprised conventional symptom control, motion, strengthening, gait, or functional training. Three neuromuscular-control outcomes underwent network meta-analysis; k ≥ 2 biomechanical comparisons were pooled and k = 1 estimates unpooled. RoB 2 assessed bias; CINeMA and GRADE assessed confidence.
RESULTS: Thirty-two trials enrolled 1437 participants. Proprioceptive training improved joint position sense versus usual rehabilitation (SMD 1.02, 95% CI 0.54-1.50; moderate CINeMA confidence); jump-landing control training yielded a favorable dynamic-balance estimate versus usual rehabilitation (1.19, 0.59-1.80; low CINeMA confidence) and was sensitive to exclusion of a late-phase multi-arm athlete trial; feedback-enhanced (0.88, 0.43-1.32) and proprioceptive training (0.59, 0.21-0.97) favored postural control (both low CINeMA confidence). Pooled estimates suggested that neuromuscular training may improve knee valgus and knee flexion kinematics during single-leg landing (1.51, 0.51-2.51; 1.07, 0.49-1.65); pooled gait biomechanical symmetry was inconclusive (-0.41, -0.87-0.05). Across networks, τ² ranged from 0.0275 to 0.1698; global tests detected no statistically clear inconsistency (P = 0.087-0.229), although sparse loop structures limited inference.
CONCLUSION: Moderate-confidence evidence supported proprioceptive training for improving joint position sense after ACLR. Other interventions may help balance and landing control, but their benefits are less certain. The evidence does not establish a single best approach across outcomes.

title: Effects of dietary nitrate supplementation in team sport athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dietary nitrate (NO3 -), typically provided as beetroot juice, increases nitric oxide availability and may reduce the oxygen cost of exercise, improve muscle oxygenation, and delay fatigue. Evidence in team sport athletes, however, remains limited and has not been comprehensively synthesized. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluate the effects of NO3 - supplementation on team sport-specific performance and related physiological and biochemical outcomes.
METHODS: This systematic review and meta-analysis followed PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO CRD42022358739). PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through March 2025 for randomized, placebo-controlled trials investigating acute (single dose) or chronic (≥2 days, with the final dose taken 2-3 h before exercise) NO3 - supplementation in male or female team sport athletes. Effect sizes (Hedges' g) were synthesized using multilevel random-effects models (REML) with cluster-robust standard errors. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB 2.0 and certainty of evidence using GRADE. Robustness analyses, including sensitivity to assumed within-person correlations for crossover trials and Monte Carlo simulations to examine the stability of key contrasts under sparse evidence were performed.
RESULTS: Twenty-four trials (n = 365 athletes; 277 males, 88 females) met inclusion criteria. Supplementation increased circulating and salivary NO3 -/NO2 -, indicating elevated systemic concentrations. The overall pooled ergogenic effect on performance was small but statistically significant (g = 0.075; 95% CI 0.026-0.124; p = 0.005). In team sport-specific tasks, NO3 - supplementation produced a small but consistent improvement with low heterogeneity and moderate certainty of evidence (g = 0.143; 95% CI 0.041-0.245; p = 0.011). A significant benefit was observed with chronic protocols (g = 0.145; 95% CI 0.076-0.214; p < 0.001), whereas acute protocols showed no clear effects. The chronic-acute contrast was statistically significant (g = 0.118; 95% CI 0.029-0.207; p = 0.013) but was not robust to more conservative crossover-correlation assumptions, lowering certainty to very low; because chronic protocols also included a final pre-exercise dose, this contrast should not be interpreted as evidence of long-term adaptation. Improvements were most evident in team sport-specific performance tests (moderate certainty), with additional, less certain signals in repeated high-intensity efforts and fatigue-sensitive neuromuscular outcomes (both very low certainty), while single-sprint outcomes and most metabolic/biochemical markers showed no consistent benefit. Cardiorespiratory responses were largely unchanged. Dose-response meta-regressions did not reveal consistent linear or non-linear trends.
CONCLUSIONS: NO3 - supplementation provides small, context-dependent ergogenic benefits in team sport athletes, most consistently for team sport-specific performance (moderate certainty), with preliminary signals for repeated high-intensity efforts and fatigue-sensitive neuromuscular performance (both very low certainty). Evidence for moderation by protocol type, sex, and training status remains suggestive but uncertain and is currently insufficient to support specific dosing recommendations. Well-powered, standardized, sex-stratified trials with harmonized outcome measures are needed to clarify key moderators and strengthen applied guidance.

title: The addition of remplissage to arthroscopic labral repair is associated with lower rates of recurrent instability and higher rates of return to sport for patients with on-track Hill-Sachs lesions: a systematic review and meta-analysis of comparative studies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite being initially described for off-track Hill-Sachs lesions (HSLs), the addition of remplissage to arthroscopic labral repair (ALR) for on-track HSL continues to generate significant interest. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to evaluate outcomes for ALR with and without remplissage for on-track HSL.
METHODS: A preregistered Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis was performed using PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL from database inception until October 23, 2025. Inclusion criteria were comparative studies for ALR with remplissage (ALR + R group) vs. ALR alone without remplissage (ALR group) for on-track HSL. Primary outcomes included recurrent instability events, return to sport, and revision surgery. A random effects meta-analysis with relative risk (RR) was conducted.
RESULTS: Eight articles were included out of 170 retrieved. Patients (n = 928; mean age: 24.0 years; 79.1% male; follow-up: 33.5 months; distance-to-dislocation: 14.2 mm; Hill-Sachs interval: 9.6 mm; percent of glenoid bone loss: 3.8%) were stratified into ALR + R (n = 298) and ALR (n = 630) groups. ALR + R patients had a 72% lower risk of recurrent instability events compared to ALR patients (RR: 0.28; P < .001; 3.4% vs. 16.0%). Among contact athletes only, the recurrent instability rate was 2.0% (n = 1) in the ALR + R group (n = 50) and 16.7% (n = 9) in the ALR group (n = 54). There was a statistically significant 15% higher risk of return to sport in the ALR + R group as compared to patients in the ALR group (RR: 1.15; P = .003; 76.3% vs. 68.9%). There was no difference in revision rates for the ALR + R group despite a greater than 4-fold higher revision rate in the ALR group (P = .08; 1.6% vs. 7.4%). Certainty of evidence for all analyses was "very low" due to the quality of evidence.
CONCLUSION: The addition of remplissage to ALR for on-track HSL appears to have clinically and statistically significant benefits for reducing the risk of post-operative recurrent instability events as well as promoting higher rates of return to sport, despite very low certainty of evidence. Future randomized controlled trials are needed for corroboration.

title: Effects of Ischemic Preconditioning on Post-exercise Injury Biomarkers, DOMS, and Endothelial Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute exercise, particularly at high intensity, confers physiological benefits but may also cause tissue injury. The protective effects of ischemic preconditioning (IPC) in clinical medicine have been demonstrated in some studies. This systematic review evaluated whether IPC applied before exercise can attenuate exercise-induced injury markers, muscle soreness, and endothelial dysfunction.
METHODS: Five databases were searched for peer-reviewed English-language studies published up to 29 June 2025. Three reviewers independently screened records using participants, intervention, control, outcome, study (PICOS) criteria for eligibility and assessed the risk of bias using Cochrane Risk of bias (RoB) 2 and Risk of Bias In Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I). Multilevel meta-analyses with cluster-robust variance adjustments were used to compare IPC with control conditions, with pooled effects reported as effect sizes (ES). Publication bias was evaluated using Egger's test. Evidence certainty was rated with Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE).
RESULTS: A total of 13 studies (3 RCTs randomized controlled trials, 9 crossover, and 1 cross-sectional) with 263 participants (243 male, 20 female) were included. IPC significantly reduced delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) overall (ES = - 0.92, 95% CI - 1.83, - 0.01, p = 0.049), but only when applied locally (LIPC, ES = - 1.16, 95% CI - 1.82, - 0.50, p < 0.01) at 24 h (ES = - 1.04, p = 0.048) and 48 h (ES = - 1.16, p = 0.03) post-exercise. A favorable pooled effect on flow-mediated dilation was observed across heterogeneous protocols involving acute remote ischemic preconditioning (RIPC), an acute comparison of LIPC with RIPC, and repeated LIPC (ES = 0.98, 95% CI 0.11-1.84, p = 0.03). No significant effects were observed for total creatine kinase (total CK, ES = - 0.38, 95% CI - 1.26, 0.50, p = 0.32) or cardiac troponin following RIPC (ES = 0.08, 95% CI - 1.79, 1.96, p = 0.86). No significant improvements in total CK were observed for acute or repeated IPC, LIPC, or RIPC (p > 0.05). Meta-regression identified recovery time as a significant moderator for cardiac troponin T (β = 0.02, p = 0.02).
CONCLUSIONS: This meta-analysis is the first to systematically find that the protective effects of IPC can extend to certain exercise-induced injuries. Pre-exercise LIPC attenuated DOMS for up to 48 h, especially after high-intensity eccentric exercise, and may provide some protection against exercise-induced endothelial dysfunction. IPC did not significantly attenuate exercise-induced increases in injury biomarkers, although protective effects may emerge at later timepoints. Overall, IPC shows potential as a protective strategy against exercise-induced injury in sports medicine. However, the magnitude of its effects, optimal protocols, and the reliability of chronic application require confirmation in larger, higher-quality studies.

title: Lower-limb performance and muscle soreness after short-term dark chocolate intake in CrossFit®-trained women: an exploratory secondary analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dark chocolate (DC) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for exercise performance and recovery, but evidence in trained women remains limited. This exploratory secondary analysis examined selected lower-limb performance outcomes and delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) in female CrossFit® athletes.
METHODS: This secondary analysis included 15 trained female CrossFit® athletes from a randomized crossover trial. No separate a priori sample-size calculation was performed for these outcomes (minimum detectable paired effect, d_z = 0.78). DC (30 g/day, 85% cocoa), placebo chocolate (PLA), and an open-label control (CONN) were compared at four operationally defined menstrual-cycle assessments after three days of supplementation. DC-PLA allocation was blinded, but blinding success was not assessed. Outcomes were vertical jump height (VJH), knee isokinetic and isometric performance, and muscle-specific DOMS after the Cindy WOD.
RESULTS: Condition effects survived FDR control for VJH and 19 of 22 dynamometry outcomes. Across assessments, VJH was 34.48 ± 5.09 cm with DC and 30.22 ± 2.34 cm with PLA (mean difference 4.27 cm, 95% CI 1.45 to 7.08; Holm-adjusted p = 0.017; g_av = 1.09). No condition-by-assessment interaction survived FDR control (all q ≥ 0.141). DOMS showed significant time effects for all three muscles, peaked at approximately 24 h, remained elevated at 48 h, and declined toward baseline by 72 h. A condition-by-time effect remained significant only for gastrocnemius soreness (Holm-adjusted p = 0.012; ηp2 = 0.212); no DOMS condition main effect or condition-by-assessment-by-time interaction was supported.
CONCLUSION: DC was associated with higher values for selected lower-limb outcomes, but these exploratory findings do not establish phase-specific efficacy, equivalent effects across cycle assessments, or a consistent DOMS benefit. Unusually large performance estimates and unmodeled period and carryover effects warrant caution.

title: Arthroscopy-Assisted Lower Trapezius Tendon Transfer Provides Superior Midterm Outcomes and Return to Work/Sport Compared With Latissimus Dorsi Tendon Transfer for Irreparable Posterosuperior Rotator Cuff Tears.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare midterm return to work (RTW) and return to sport (RTS) rates, clinical outcomes, muscle strength, and radiologic survivorship between arthroscopy-assisted lower trapezius tendon transfer (aLTT) and arthroscopy-assisted latissimus dorsi tendon transfer (aLDT) in patients with posterosuperior irreparable rotator cuff tears.
METHODS: This retrospective comparative study included patients who underwent aLDT or aLTT for posterosuperior irreparable rotator cuff tears between January 2012 and October 2020, with a minimum follow-up of 5 years. The primary outcomes were RTW and RTS rates. Secondary clinical outcomes included patient-reported outcome measures, active range of motion, and active range of motion strength. Radiological outcomes included acromiohumeral distance and Hamada grade. Graft integrity was assessed using postoperative magnetic resonance imaging. Factors associated with RTW and RTS were identified using multivariate logistic regression analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 94 patients were divided into 2 groups according to the surgical procedure: the aLDT group (n = 44) underwent aLDT, and the aLTT group (n = 50) underwent aLTT. The aLTT group showed significantly higher RTW (90.0% vs 72.7%, P = .035) and RTS (88.6% vs 63.3%, P = .020) rates than the aLDT group. Both groups showed significant postoperative improvements in clinical outcomes. Postoperative Constant scores (50.7 ± 11.0 vs 64.8 ± 12.8, P < .001), American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons scores (70.5 ± 10.8 vs 83.8 ± 11.8, P < .001), Activities of Daily Living requiring External Rotation scores (20.6 ± 5.7 vs 25.7 ± 3.9, P < .001), forward elevation (135.7° ± 31.7° vs 153.3° ± 22.5°, P = .005), external rotation at the side (34.1° ± 9.5° vs 54.4° ± 22.9°, P < .001), forward elevation strength (20.4 ± 4.2 N vs 24.5 ± 4.4 N, P < .001), and external rotation strength (19.3 ± 3.7 N vs 23.9 ± 4.8 N, P < .001) were all significantly higher in the aLTT group compared with the aLDT group. The progression of arthritic changes was significantly greater in the aLDT group (50%) compared with the aLTT group (12%) (P < .001). Postoperative forward elevation strength, external rotation strength, and progression of arthritic changes were independently associated with higher odds of RTW and RTS.
CONCLUSIONS: aLTT showed superior RTW and RTS outcomes compared with aLDT at midterm follow-up. These functional advantages were accompanied by greater clinical improvements and more favorable radiologic parameters, reflecting the biomechanical superiority of the aLTT.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.

title: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation combined with resistance exercise for knee osteoarthritis: randomized clinical trial protocol.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Resistance exercise is the gold-standard conservative treatment for knee osteoarthritis (KOA). However, arthrogenic muscle inhibition and quadriceps weakness may limit the effectiveness of strengthening programs. Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) has been proposed as an adjunct strategy to enhance muscle activation, yet current evidence in KOA remains inconclusive and methodologically limited.
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the effects of adding NMES, applied concurrently with voluntary contractions, to a resistance exercise program in individuals with KOA.
METHODS: This double-blind, parallel-group randomized controlled trial will include 84 participants with clinically diagnosed KOA, randomly allocated (1:1) to resistance exercise combined with either active or sham NMES. Both groups will perform supervised sessions twice weekly for eight weeks. The primary outcome will be knee pain assessed by the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS). Secondary outcomes will include self-reported physical function, knee extensor torque, performance-based physical function, and adverse events. Assessments will be conducted at baseline, post-intervention, and 12-week follow-up. Data will be analyzed using linear mixed models under the intention-to-treat principle.
CONCLUSION: This study may clarify whether adding NMES provides additional therapeutic benefits in KOA rehabilitation and support evidence-based clinical decision-making.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: ensaiosclinicos.gov.br identifier is RBR-77f8rjq.

title: Effectiveness of a Structured Post-Platelet Rich Plasma Rehabilitation Approach on Pain and Function in Subacromial Pain Syndrome: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Subacromial pain syndrome (SAPS) causes pain and functional limitation. Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) is increasingly used as a supportive treatment. Optimal rehabilitation after PRP is unclear. This study investigated the effectiveness of a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach on pain and function.
METHODS: Sixty participants with SAPS were randomized to two groups; 54 completed the study and were included in the final per-protocol analysis (27 per group). During a 21-day period, the study group received a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach in addition to standard conventional physiotherapy, while the control group received standard conventional physiotherapy alone. Range of motion, muscle strength, and posture were evaluated. In addition, outcome measures included the Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire (SF-MPQ), Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand Questionnaire (DASH), Functional Impairment Test-Hand and Neck/Shoulder/Arm (FIT-HaNSA) and Constant-Murley Shoulder Score, which were administered for assessment purposes.
RESULTS: Corbin Posture Scale scores decreased in both groups (p < 0.05). Pain reduction was greater in the study group (VAS: from 9.00 ± 0.67 to 2.92 ± 1.14 versus from 9.11 ± 0.64 to 7.96 ± 0.75; SF-MPQ: from 27.07 ± 4.41 to 10.07 ± 3.33 versus from 21.33 ± 2.46 to 19.37 ± 2.35; p < 0.001). Improvements in Constant-Murley, DASH, and FIT-HaNSA scores, shoulder muscle strength, and active and passive range of motion were significantly greater in the study group (p < 0.001).
DISCUSSION: Adding a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach to standard conventional physiotherapy may provide additional short-term improvements in pain, muscle strength, range of motion, and shoulder function compared with standard conventional physiotherapy alone in individuals with SAPS. However, long-term follow-up was not conducted. Therefore, the sustainability of the observed improvements remains unclear. Future studies should investigate the long-term effects of structured post-PRP rehabilitation approaches.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT07410208; registered on January 21, 2026.

title: Muscle Activation, Pain and Disability Changes With Rehabilitation Interventions in Patients With Rotator Cuff Tendinopathy: A Systematic Review.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To synthesize evidence on concurrent changes in electromyographic (EMG) muscle activation and pain or disability after rehabilitation for rotator cuff tendinopathy. DESIGN: Systematic review. LITERATURE SEARCH: MEDLINE, CENTRAL, and PEDro (inception to October 2026), reference lists, and expert consultation. STUDY SELECTION CRITERIA: Randomized and non-randomized studies of adults with rotator cuff tendinopathy, including subacromial impingement or pain syndrome, reporting EMG activation and patient-reported pain or disability before and after rehabilitation. DATA SYNTHESIS: Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias (RoB 2, ROBINS-I), EMG reporting quality, and certainty of evidence (GRADE). Findings were synthesized descriptively, prioritizing randomized between-group comparisons. RESULTS: Twenty-two studies (828 participants; 12 randomized trials) were included. EMG changes were inconsistent: upper trapezius activation decreased in 6 of 20 studies and increased in 5; lower trapezius and serratus anterior activation each increased in 5 and decreased in 4. Pain or disability improved in 19 studies, with or without EMG changes. In 6 randomized trials, adding a component intended to change muscle activation did not further improve pain or disability despite between-group EMG differences in 4. Greater EMG change coincided with greater clinical improvement in 3 of 11 comparisons. Only 2 studies had low risk of bias for patient-reported outcomes; certainty of evidence was low to very low. CONCLUSION: Muscle activation changes did not consistently accompany improvements in pain or disability, and adding components that changed muscle activation did not improve outcomes further. Normalizing muscle activation should not be assumed necessary for recovery.

title: Efficacy of Physical Activity Interventions in Athletic Rehabilitation for Musculoskeletal Injuries: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Sports injuries involving the musculoskeletal system are highly prevalent and can prolong recovery and increase the likelihood of reinjury. This systematic review evaluated the effectiveness of physical activity-based rehabilitation for athletes with musculoskeletal injuries, synthesizing data from 50 studies published between August 2010 and December 2025 across seven databases, including randomized controlled trials, prospective cohort studies, systematic reviews, and clinical practice guidelines. They covered a range of athletes, from recreational to elite, and various injuries, including anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction, ankle sprains, hamstring strains, groin injuries, tendinopathy, shoulder impingement, and patellofemoral pain. Strength training, neuromuscular training, balance training, aerobic training, aquatic training, and sport-specific training were among the interventions; pain, function, strength, neuromuscular control, and return to sport were among the outcome measures. Consistent relationships between interventions and improvements in functional and return-to-sport outcomes were found with consistent, progressive interventions; some individual studies found a 41-63% relative reduction in the risk of injury or reinjury. There was substantial variation between protocols and outcomes, so findings were synthesized narratively rather than pooled. Results demonstrate the need for evidence-based programming, an individualized approach, and standardized reporting in future trials.

title: Lateral Femoral Condyle Osteochondral Allograft Transplantation Location for Osteochondral Defects of the Knee Is Associated With Selected Patient-Reported Outcome Differences but Not With Graft Reoperation or Failure.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), clinically significant outcome achievement, reoperation, and graft failure after isolated medial femoral condyle (MFC) and lateral femoral condyle (LFC) osteochondral allograft (OCA) transplantation.
METHODS: Consecutive patients who underwent OCA at a single cartilage restoration center from 2003 to 2023 were reviewed. Patients were included if they underwent isolated MFC or LFC OCA transplantation and had preoperative and minimum 2-year postoperative PROMs. When multiple postoperative PROMs were available, the most recent score at or beyond 2 years was used. Cohort-specific minimal clinically important difference (MCID) thresholds were calculated as one-half the standard deviation of the change score. Multivariable linear and logistic regression models were adjusted for graft location, baseline PROM score, follow-up time, age, sex, Workers' Compensation status, athlete status, and laterality. Time to reoperation was compared with Kaplan-Meier/log-rank analysis and Cox regression.
RESULTS: A total of 141 patients were included (MFC: n = 79; LFC: n = 62). Follow-up data were available for 115 patients and averaged 6.2 ± 3.0 years (range, 2.0-16.3 years), with no difference between MFC and LFC cohorts (6.2 ± 2.9 vs 6.2 ± 3.2 years; P = .963). In adjusted linear models accounting for baseline PROM score, follow-up time, age, sex, Workers' Compensation status, athlete status, laterality, and ipsilateral meniscal allograft transplantation status, the LFC recipient site was associated with higher Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) Pain (β = 9.1; 95% confidence interval, 1.2-16.9; P = .024) and KOOS Quality of Life (QoL) (β = 12.3; 95% confidence interval, 1.6-23.0; P = .025) scores. After the same adjustment, the LFC recipient site was associated with greater odds of achieving cohort-specific MCID for KOOS QoL, whereas the corresponding KOOS Pain MCID association was attenuated to nonsignificance (P = .054) once ipsilateral meniscal allograft transplantation was included in the model; other threshold analyses were not significantly different. Reoperation rates were 27.8% for MFC and 29.0% for LFC (log-rank P = .805). Graft failure was rare (MFC, 2.5%; LFC, 0%; P = .504).
CONCLUSIONS: At a minimum 2-year follow-up, the LFC OCA recipient site was associated with higher adjusted KOOS Pain and KOOS QoL scores and higher adjusted odds of achieving cohort-specific MCID for KOOS QoL, an association that persisted after adjusting for ipsilateral meniscal allograft transplantation status. Graft location was not associated with reoperation or graft failure.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: Association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden in NCAA Division I athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden among NCAA Division I athletes and whether sleep difficulty is associated with neurocognitive performance.
METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis included 584 NCAA Division I student-athletes. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire Sleep Difficulty Score (SDS), and symptom burden using the 24-item SCOAT6 Symptom Evaluation. Symptom number was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression and symptom severity with multivariable linear regression using HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age, sex, sport type, and head-injury history. Sensitivity analyses excluded overlapping sleep-related symptoms and examined individual symptoms, symptom domains, head-injury strata, and neurocognitive outcomes.
RESULTS: Each 1-point increase in SDS was associated with greater symptom number (n = 583; IRR = 1.127, 95% CI 1.086-1.169, P < .001) and severity (n = 584; B = 1.054, 95% CI 0.688-1.419, P < .001). Associations persisted after excluding sleep disturbance and after additionally excluding fatigue/low energy and drowsiness. Twenty-one of 24 symptoms remained associated with SDS after false-discovery-rate correction. Head-injury history did not modify associations with symptom number (P = .971) or severity (P = .846). SDS was not associated with memory (B = -0.012, P = .269), executive function (B = -0.017, P = .247), or psychomotor speed (B = 0.001, P = .939).
CONCLUSIONS: Greater self-reported sleep difficulty was associated with greater baseline concussion-like symptom burden but not with assessed neurocognitive outcomes. Sleep difficulty should be considered a contextual factor when interpreting baseline concussion symptom reports.

title: Anterior cruciate ligament injuries in women's professional football: Higher incidence and distinct injury patterns compared to men.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are more frequent in female football players, but sex-specific differences in injury characteristics remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to analyse sex-specific differences in ACL injury incidence and characteristics in professional football.
METHODS: This prospective cohort study used data from a German national ACL registry ('Kreuzbandregister im Deutschen Fußball'), including professional male (first to third league) and female (first and second league) football players from the 2016/2017 to 2024/2025 seasons. Incidence rates were compared using Poisson regression (incidence rate ratio, IRR) and injury characteristics using multivariable logistic regression.
RESULTS: A total of 459 ACL injuries were analysed (177 female and 282 male). The rate was 1.19 versus 0.69 per 1000 match hours (IRR 1.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.34-2.13). The difference was most pronounced in the first division (IRR 2.49, 1.82-3.41) and smaller and not significant in the lower leagues (IRR 1.24, 0.93-1.65). Injuries in female players were more often non-contact (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.37) and indirect-contact injuries (aOR 2.92), occurred more often on artificial turf (aOR 5.42) and in national team players (aOR 3.03). Concomitant injury patterns did not differ significantly, except for fewer lateral collateral ligament injuries in women.
CONCLUSION: ACL injury rates are higher in female professional football players, particularly in the first division. The predominance of non-contact and indirect-contact mechanisms supports targeted, sex-specific prevention strategies.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, prospective cohort study.

title: Repeated-Sprint Training in Hypoxia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis with Exploratory Dose-Response Modeling.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Repeated-sprint training in hypoxia may improve repeated-sprint performance, but the relationship between external hypoxic exposure and adaptation remains unclear.
OBJECTIVES: To quantify the effects of repeated-sprint training in hypoxia (RSH) on repeated-sprint performance near sea level and examine the hypoxic dose-response relationship using both frequentist and Bayesian approaches.
METHODS: Eight databases were systematically searched for randomized-controlled trials comparing RSH with matched repeated-sprint training in normoxia (RSN). Best (RSAbest) and mean (RSAmean) repeated-sprint performance were synthesized using frequentist and Bayesian random-effects meta-analyses, with exploratory study-level dose-response modeling. Risk of bias was assessed using the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (RoB 2), and certainty using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework.
RESULTS: Twenty-one studies met the eligibility criteria. RSH produced small effects on RSAbest (k = 16; g = 0.24, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.00 to 0.48; I2 = 16.2%) and RSAmean (k = 20; g = 0.31, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.53; I2 = 13.6%). Bayesian analyses supported these findings, with probabilities of benefit of 98.4% and 99.9%, respectively. Dose-response analyses identified no consistent linear or nonlinear association between cumulative external hypoxic exposure and either outcome, nor any consistent optimal hypoxic dose.
CONCLUSIONS: This meta-analysis indicates that repeated-sprint training in hypoxia may produce small improvements in both best and mean repeated-sprint performance, supported by both frequentist and Bayesian analyses. Study-level analyses identified neither a consistent linear or nonlinear association between training-structured external hypoxic exposure and performance nor an optimal hypoxic dose. Future trials should standardize repeated-sprint outcomes and report continuous or high-frequency peripheral oxygen saturation alongside mechanical training output to better characterize the effective hypoxic dose. title: Effects of a commercially available sugar-free energy drink on hitting exit velocity in experienced baseball and softball players: a randomized crossover trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Caffeine is commonly used as an ergogenic aid, with effective doses often reported at approximately 3-9 mg/kg; however, lower doses are also frequently included in multi-ingredient pre-workout supplements, and the effects of these supplements on sport-specific hitting performance in baseball and softball players remain largely unexplored. Thus, we investigated the acute effects of a commercially available, multi-ingredient caffeinated energy drink (ED) on hitting exit velocity, countermovement jump (CMJ) height, barbell velocity, reaction time, perceived energy, and post-running metabolic outcomes in experienced baseball and softball players.
METHODS: Twenty-two experienced baseball and softball players (14 males, 8 females; mean playing experience: 13 ± 2 years) completed this double-blind, randomized, crossover study. Participants consumed either a sugar-free and caffeinated ED (C4 Performance Energy®; 5 kcal, 200 mg caffeine, β-alanine, betaine anhydrous, and vitamin B12) or a low-calorie, flavor-matched placebo (PLA) during two experimental sessions separated by ≥ 5 days. Testing batteries were performed at three within-session timepoints (T0: pre-consumption; T1: 30 minutes post-consumption; T2: post-exercise) and included CMJs, 30 back squat repetitions at 30% of estimated 1RM, a computerized reaction time test, and subjective perceptual questionnaires. Participants also performed 40 tee hits after T1 and before a high-intensity interval treadmill protocol, followed by 15-minute post-exercise indirect calorimetry.
RESULTS: Both average (ED: 71.3 ± 14.0 mph vs. PLA: 70.1 ± 13.5 mph; mean difference ± SD: 1.20 ± 1.41 mph, 95% CI: 0.56-1.84, p < 0.001, dz = 0.85) and peak (ED: 76.7 ± 13.9 mph vs. PLA: 75.1 ± 13.6 mph; mean difference ± SD: 1.56 ± 1.70 mph, 95% CI: 0.79-2.33, p < 0.001, dz = 0.92) hitting exit velocity were significantly greater in the ED condition. A significant condition × time interaction was observed for CMJ height (p = 0.003), whereby jump height was maintained with the ED condition but decreased with PLA at T1. Post-exercise recovery energy expenditure was significantly greater with ED (~5%; p = 0.040, d = 0.46). No significant interactions were observed for barbell velocity, reaction time, or subjective perceptual questionnaires.
CONCLUSIONS: Acute consumption of a caffeinated multi-ingredient energy drink resulted in small increases in average and peak hitting exit velocity and attenuated transient decline in CMJ height observed with placebo. These findings warrant future investigations with live-pitching conditions in prolonged game simulation settings.

title: Recovery of Running and Technical Match Performance After Adductor Muscle Strain Injury in Male Professional Football Players: A Prospective Cohort Study of 27 Players From One LaLiga Team Across Five Seasons.
abstract: Post return-to-play (RTP) running and technical match performance after adductor muscle strain injury remains unclear. The aim of the present study was to examine recovery of running and technical match performance after RTP following acute adductor muscle strain injury in professional football. This prospective longitudinal cohort study followed players from one team (n = 122) across five seasons (2020/2021-2024/2025). Injuries were recorded by the medical staff and confirmed by magnetic resonance imaging. Match performance variables included playing time, total distance, high-speed running distance (> 24 km/h), number of sprints (> 24 km/h), and offensive and defensive technical actions. First eight matches following RTP were compared with the four pre-injury matches. RTP required unrestricted team training and medical clearance for match selection. Data were analyzed using generalized estimating equations methods, adjusting event counts for the amount of playing time. Of the 122 players, 27 sustained at least one acute adductor muscle strain injury, accounting for 54 injury episodes. At Match 1, time played was -7.1% versus PRE (95% CI -16.7% to +3.5%), total-distance rate -0.4% (-2.4% to +1.5%), high-speed running distance +6.9% (-3.5% to +18.5%), and number of sprints +5.9% (-4.0% to +16.8%); none remained significant after FDR adjustment (p ≥ 0.182; pFDR ≥ 0.817). At Match 8, total passes were 26.5% below PRE (95% CI -50.0% to +7.9%; raw p = 0.116; pFDR = 0.567). Across all Match 1-8 contrasts, only long passes at Match 3 remained significant after FDR adjustment (-15.3%; 95% CI -22.4% to -7.6%; raw p < 0.001; pFDR = 0.022). In conclusion, there was little evidence of systematic population-level impairment in running or technical match performance after RTP. Late passing reductions warrant confirmation in larger independent cohorts.

title: Risk, Knowledge, and Awareness of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S) in Elite Female Volleyball Players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a condition caused by low energy availability (LEA) and is associated with adverse health and performance outcomes in athletes. Although volleyball involves considerable physical stress and repetitive jumping, little is known about RED-S knowledge and risk of LEA in elite female volleyball players.
HYPOTHESIS: Elite female volleyball athletes have limited awareness of RED-S, and athletes at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q are more likely to be injured.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Elite female volleyball athletes competing in the Turkish Women's Elite Volleyball League during the 2024-2025 season were recruited. Participants completed an online survey including demographic information, the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q), and items assessing knowledge, awareness, and support-seeking behaviors related to RED-S. Athletes were classified as "at risk" for LEA using a LEAF-Q cutoff score of ≥8. Associations between LEAF-Q risk status and injury history during the previous year were analyzed.
RESULTS: A total of 148 athletes participated. The mean LEAF-Q score was 5.50 ± 3.48, and 25% of athletes were classified as at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q. Most athletes (92.6%) reported never having heard of RED-S or the Female Athlete Triad. Athletes identified as at risk by the LEAF-Q were significantly more likely to have sustained an injury in the previous year than athletes not at risk (odds ratio, 7.86; 95% CI, 3.03-20.41).
CONCLUSION: Elite female volleyball athletes demonstrated low knowledge of RED-S, while a substantial proportion were identified as at risk for LEA. LEA risk was associated strongly with injury history, supporting the clinical relevance of LEAF-Q screening in this population.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine LEAF-Q screening combined with sport-specific education may facilitate early identification of athletes who may require further clinical evaluation for LEA-related problems and may inform prevention-oriented support strategies in elite female volleyball players.

title: Minimally Invasive Surgery for Insertional Achilles Tendinopathy Using a Double-Row SpeedBridge Repair with Rip-Stop Augmentation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The present video article describes a minimally invasive surgery (MIS) technique utilizing a double-row rip-stop SpeedBridge (Arthrex) repair for the treatment of insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT). This procedure is utilized when nonoperative treatment has failed, with the goal of returning patients to their previous levels of activity while avoiding the complications associated with more open procedures. All products mentioned in the videos are manufactured by Arthrex.
DESCRIPTION: The surgical technique is performed with 4 small incisions-2 distal and 2 proximal. Any Haglund deformity and/or enthesophyte are resected with use of an MIS burr through the 2 distal portals. The central third of the Achilles tendon is partially detached with this resection and is repaired with use of a double-row repair. Proximal anchors are placed, and sutures are passed through the Achilles tendon. Working knotless sutures are tensioned to create a rip-stop suture. The sutures are passed and shuttled to the distal row, creating a double-row repair. The distal row is drilled and tapped. The double-row repair is completed with insertion of distal anchors under appropriate tension.
ALTERNATIVES: Nonoperative treatment is beneficial in the initial stages of the condition and is successful in 60% to 80% of patients1-3. Initial treatment strategies for IAT include RICE (rest, ice, compression, and elevation), nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and physical therapy. Eccentric exercise and extracorporeal shockwave therapy have shown promising results3. Paratendinous injections, such as with platelet-rich plasma, have shown various levels of success and need further evaluation3. When nonoperative treatment has failed, operative treatment is a viable option. The surgical approach should be chosen on a patient-specific basis, as different tendinopathy patterns and different associated osseous and soft-tissue conditions may influence preoperative planning. There are a variety of different surgical techniques that include open, endoscopic, and MIS procedures.
RATIONALE: This MIS technique utilizing a double-row SpeedBridge repair with rip-stop augmentation yields fewer wound complications, less pain, quicker initiation of rehabilitation protocols, and quicker return to sport compared with more invasive techniques. Furthermore, the addition of the rip-stop augment to the double-row SpeedBridge repair improves dynamic mechanical strength and mitigates suture tearing through the tendon4.
EXPECTED OUTCOMES: In our experience, patients who undergo this technique will be weight-bearing in a controlled-ankle-motion boot immediately postoperatively and out of the boot by 6 weeks postoperatively, with progressive return to full activities as tolerated. Our study of 61 patients undergoing the double-row SpeedBridge repair demonstrated favorable outcomes, with Foot and Ankle Disability Index scores improving from a mean of 56.3 preoperatively to 98.62 at 12 months postoperatively and visual analog scale pain scores improving from a mean of 7.25 to 0.476. There were no postoperative ruptures at a mean follow-up of 12.5 months. Eleven patients had minor complications within 3 months, including 6 who reported some central numbness over the Achilles tendon6. We expect these outcomes to improve as surgeons become more comfortable and skilled performing MIS techniques.
IMPORTANT TIPS: Proper patient selection (chronic IAT with Haglund deformity and/or an enthesophyte) will help ensure optimal outcomes.It is important to develop a subcutaneous plane for suture passage.The use of fluoroscopy or a nanoscope is helpful in ensuring that the proper bone is resected with the MIS burr.We have found that the irrigator from the MIS burr can be utilized alongside a Frazier suction tip to help remove excess bone.Suture management is important. Precisely maneuver the sutures at all times; it is very important that the sutures do not get tangled so that the procedure flows efficiently.Make sure to fully tension both sutures in order to place the ripstop.
ACRONYMS AND ABBREVIATIONS: NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugMRI = magnetic resonance imagingK-wire = Kirschner wireCI = confidence intervalBID = twice dailyprn = as neededDVT = deep vein thrombosis.

title: Cognitive Muscular Therapy plus usual care versus usual care alone for people with clinically diagnosed knee osteoarthritis: protocol for a multicentre randomised controlled trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Many people with knee osteoarthritis (OA) remain symptomatic despite undertaking guideline-recommended therapeutic exercise and subsequently progress to more invasive treatments. Cognitive Muscular Therapy (CMT) has been developed as an integrated behavioural intervention that combines psychologically informed practice with muscle biofeedback training. The aim of CMT is to reduce muscle overactivity, minimise mechanical loading on the knee and change beliefs related to knee OA pain. A previous feasibility trial demonstrated that CMT is acceptable to patients and physiotherapists and may improve pain and disability. This trial aims to evaluate the clinical and cost-effectiveness of CMT plus usual care compared with usual care alone in people with knee OA who are dissatisfied with the outcome of therapeutic exercise.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS: BEhaviour change for People with clinically diagnosed Knee Osteoarthritis (BEPKO-3) is a pragmatic, multicentre, two-arm, superiority randomised controlled trial with an embedded economic evaluation. A total of 252 participants with a clinical diagnosis of knee OA will be recruited from physiotherapy clinics, general practitioners and musculoskeletal triage services. Participants will be randomised (1:1) to receive either CMT plus usual care or usual care alone. Participants in the CMT arm will receive 7 weekly individual physiotherapy sessions. The primary outcome is the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) composite score at 12 months. Secondary outcomes include WOMAC subscales, Global Assessment of Knee Symptoms, Pain Catastrophizing Scale, Pain Self-Efficacy Questionnaire, Work Productivity and Activity Impairment Questionnaire for Osteoarthritis, EuroQol 5-Dimension 5-Level, healthcare resource use and adverse events. Outcomes will be collected at baseline, 6 months and 12 months. Statistical analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle, and a within-trial cost-utility analysis will be conducted from National health service (NHS) and personal social services perspectives.
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: The study has received approval from a UK NHS Research Ethics Committee (25/WA/0329). Findings will be published in a peer-reviewed source, and an anonymised dataset made available with the publication.

title: Arthroscopic Stabilization Reduces Recurrence but May Delay Return to Sport After First-Time Traumatic Anterior Shoulder Dislocation in Elite Male Athletes: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate arthroscopic stabilization versus nonoperative management for first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation in adult athletes, with a focus on recurrent instability, return-to-play rates, and time to return to play.
METHODS: Five databases were searched from inception to July 2025. Studies comparing arthroscopic stabilization versus nonoperative management in adult athletes (≥18 years) with first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation were included. The primary outcome was recurrent instability. Secondary outcomes included return-to-play rates and time to return to play. A narrative synthesis was performed given the nonrandomized and heterogeneous nature of included studies. Evidence certainty was assessed using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation.
RESULTS: Five studies (232 participants: 111 operative, 121 nonoperative) were included. Recurrent instability rates ranged from 3% to 14% in the operative group and 24% to 80% in the nonoperative group. Return-to-play rates were high for both approaches (operative: 93%-100%; nonoperative: 97%-100%). Nonoperative management was associated with earlier return to sport (2.3-5.7 weeks vs 18.7-39.3 weeks for operative management in studies reporting this outcome). All studies involved elite athletes, with female athletes substantially under-represented.
CONCLUSIONS: Arthroscopic stabilization was consistently associated with lower rates of recurrent instability than nonoperative management after first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation but required a longer time to return to play. Nonoperative management enabled an earlier return to play but was associated with higher recurrence. The evidence is limited primarily to male military, collegiate, and professional athletes, restricting generalizability to female, recreational, and broader adult athletic populations.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, systematic review of Level II and III studies.

title: Ischemic Preconditioning Effects in Competitive Swim Athletes: A Randomized Control Trial.
abstract: Montgomery, ME, Scholten, HG, and Scholten, SD. Ischemic preconditioning effects in competitive swim athletes: A randomized control trial. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Ischemic preconditioning (IPC) has been shown to effectively enhance athletic performance in short-duration (250 yard) swimming, possibly through mechanisms related to the vascular system. Swimming is an ideal mode of exercise to test IPC's effectiveness outside of the lab because of the controlled environment. However, it remains unclear whether these benefits persist over longer swimming distances. To address this gap, this study investigated the potential benefits of IPC on performance in a 500-yard swimming event by conducting a block-randomized controlled trial comparing swim times under 2 IPC conditions: a 1-minute sham condition and a 5-minute IPC intervention. Fourteen NCAA Division II swimmers completed all trials. Eleven out of 14 subjects swam faster (1.72 seconds) with IPC treatment than with sham treatment (p = 0.19; effect size = 0.08). This improvement in time is small, but it is worth considering in competitive sports, where the time difference among competitive athletes is small.

title: Simultaneous versus Staged Bilateral Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Retrospective Cohort Study of Surgical Outcomes and Postoperative Complications.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Knee osteoarthritis commonly presents as a bilateral condition, thereby often indicating the need for bilateral knee arthroplasty to achieve optimal therapeutic outcomes. Simultaneous bilateral knee arthroplasty has emerged as an increasingly favored treatment approach, owing to its numerous clinical advantages. This study aims to compare the clinical outcomes and complications of simultaneous bilateral total knee arthroplasty (sim-BTKA) and staged bilateral total knee arthroplasty (stag-BTKA).
METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted at Viet Duc University Hospital between November 2021 and March 2024, including 38 patients (12 sim-BTKA and 26 stag-BTKA). All procedures were performed by the same surgeon using a standardized perioperative rehabilitation protocol. Postoperative pain was assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), while functional outcomes were evaluated using the Knee Society Score (KS) and Knee Function Score (KFS). Longitudinal postoperative outcomes were analyzed using generalized estimating equations (GEE) to account for repeated measurements over time.
RESULTS: Generalized estimating equation analysis demonstrated significant improvements in VAS, KS, and KFS over time in both groups (all p < 0.001), whereas no significant group-by-time interaction was observed, indicating comparable recovery trajectories between treatment strategies. The simultaneous bilateral total knee arthroplasty (sim-BTKA) procedures were completed in markedly less time, averaging 88.75 minutes versus 104.62 minutes for the staged approach (p = 0.001). While patients undergoing sim-BTKA reported slightly greater postoperative pain based on visual analog scale (VAS) measurements during the first month, and those with staged procedures (stag-BTKA) showed better functional outcomes per Knee Society Scores (KSS) in follow-up assessments, neither trend reached statistical significance (p > 0.05). The average hospital length of stay was significantly shorter in the simultaneous BTKA group compared to the staged BTKA group (9.25 vs. 15.8 days, p = 0.02). Additionally, the total surgical costs were reduced in the simultaneous BTKA cohort ( 2 , 000 v s . 2,760, p = 0.045). No statistically significant differences in postoperative complications were detected between groups; however, the study was not powered to detect small differences in complication rates.
CONCLUSIONS: Simultaneous bilateral total knee arthroplasty (BTKA) reduces operative time, hospital stay, and surgical cost compared to staged BTKA. No statistically significant between-group differences were observed in postoperative pain, functional recovery, or complications. However, because of the limited statistical power, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence between treatment strategies. Recommendations: Simultaneous BTKA should be performed in high-capacity orthopedic surgical facilities with experienced surgeons and multidisciplinary perioperative management. Optimal patient selection is essential, prioritizing ASA I-II candidates to reduce surgical risks.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 3 (A retrospective cohort study) Ethical approval: The study was reviewed by the institutional ethics committee, which determined that formal ethical approval was not required because only anonymized retrospective clinical data were analyzed. Funding: The authors received no specific funding for this work.

title: Return to play rate and performance after ulnar collateral ligament repair with suture tape augmentation in major league baseball players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) repair with suture tape augmentation has emerged as an alternative to traditional reconstruction in appropriately selected patients. While clinical outcomes of UCL repair have been reported in amateur athletes, data evaluating performance outcomes in Major League Baseball (MLB) players remain limited. The purpose of this study was to evaluate return to play (RTP) and changes in performance metrics among MLB players undergoing UCL repair with suture tape augmentation. We hypothesized that UCL repair would allow a faster RTP compared with historical reconstruction data while maintaining player performance.
METHODS: MLB players who underwent UCL repair with suture tape augmentation between 2016 and 2024 were identified using publicly available injury databases. Player performance metrics were obtained from publicly available databases including MLB Statcast. The primary outcome was time to RTP. Secondary outcomes included traditional and advanced performance metrics. For pitchers, metrics included earned run average, innings pitched, strikeouts, walk rate, fastball velocity, fastball spin rate, fielder independent pitching, fangraphs wins above replacement (fWAR), and Statcast-based metrics. Position player metrics included fWAR, fielding run value, and arm strength. Pre-operative and post-operative metrics were compared using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests or Mann-Whitney tests with statistical significance set at P < .05.
RESULTS: Twenty-two MLB players met inclusion criteria. RTP to the MLB level was 81.8% (18/22). The mean RTP time was 10.98 months (range, 5.9-34). Pitchers had a mean RTP of 13.51 months (range, 9-34) and position players had a mean RTP of 7.51 months (range, 5.9-8.5). There were no statistically significant differences between pre-operative and post-operative performance metrics, including earned run average (3.66 ± 0.7 vs. 3.95 ± 1.9; P = .765), fastball velocity (93.0 ± 1.7 vs. 92.7 ± 1.9 mph; P = .609), innings pitched (42.1 ± 39.0 vs. 23.0 ± 28.0; P = .266), strikeouts (31.7 ± 53.7 vs. 23.5 ± 27.4; P = .247), or fastball spin rate (2,241 ± 131 vs. 2,235 ± 122 rpm; P = .496). Similarly, position players demonstrated no significant differences in fWAR, fielding run value, or arm strength after RTP.
CONCLUSION: UCL repair with suture tape augmentation in MLB players demonstrates a high rate of RTP with preservation of traditional and advanced performance metrics. Position players returned earlier than pitchers; overall RTP remained favorable. UCL repair with suture tape augmentation provides an effective surgical option allowing return to elite-level performance.

title: Platelet Concentrates in Tooth Replantation: A Narrative Review and Evidence Synthesis of Periodontal and Pulpal Healing.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: The prognosis of an avulsed, replanted tooth over the long term hinges on whether the periodontal ligament (PDL) and the dental pulp can be preserved or regenerated. When extra-oral dry time is prolonged, PDL necrosis follows, and the root becomes prone to inflammatory or replacement (ankylotic) resorption. Platelet concentrates-platelet-rich plasma (PRP), leukocyte- and platelet-rich plasma (L-PRP), and platelet-rich fibrin (PRF)-are autologous biomaterials that supply growth factors and may influence this healing process. This review asks whether autologous platelet concentrates reduce inflammatory and replacement (ankylotic) root resorption and improve periodontal and pulpal healing after delayed or intentional tooth replantation, compared with no adjunct, and whether residual periodontal ligament (PDL) viability changes this effect.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: This narrative synthesis (not a systematic review) draws together recent controlled clinical and animal studies with the case-report and preclinical literature already captured in the only published systematic review on this topic. The search covered PubMed, Google Scholar, the Cochrane Library, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, from January to May 2026.
RESULTS: In preclinical models, L-PRP and PRF promote pulpal repair, tertiary dentin formation, and attenuated inflammatory root resorption, although neither consistently prevents ankylosis once PDL viability has been lost. In one retrospective comparative study of intentional replantation in hopeless teeth, PRF combined with root-surface biomodification produced greater clinical attachment gain and a larger reduction in probing depth than replantation alone, a direction consistent with earlier case reports. Small, largely non-randomized samples and unstandardized protocols still limit this evidence.
CONCLUSIONS: Platelet concentrates are biologically plausible adjuncts that improve periodontal and pulpal healing indices, yet they do not reliably prevent ankylosis. Their clinical role will remain undefined until prospective randomized trials with standardized protocols are available.

title: Pulsed electromagnetic fields therapy is associated with reduced perioperative pain after ACL reconstruction in patients with concomitant bone bruise: A randomised controlled trial.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Bone bruise (BB) is common after acute anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury, but its relationship with pain and recovery is variable. This randomised controlled trial evaluated whether perioperative pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) stimulation improves pain control and recovery after ACL reconstruction (ACL-R) in patients with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-confirmed BB. We hypothesised that PEMF stimulation would reduce pain, improve patient-reported outcomes and promote BB volume reduction.
METHODS: Ninety-two patients were enrolled: 66 completed follow-up and were analysed (31 PEMF, 35 control). The PEMF group was prescribed a wearable device for 4 h/day from 20 days before surgery through 60 days postoperatively. Outcomes included visual analogue scale (VAS) pain, International Knee Documentation Committee, knee injury and osteoarthritis outcome score, SF-12 Health Survey (SF-12), Tegner activity score, analgesic/nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, and MRI-estimated BB volume. Clinical follow-up was performed at diagnosis, immediately before surgery, and at 2, 6 and 12 months; MRI was obtained preoperatively and at 2, 6 and 12 months.
RESULTS: VAS pain was lower in the PEMF group preoperatively (1.7 ± 1.9 vs. 2.7 ± 2.4; p = 0.033), at 6 months (0.5 ± 0.8 vs. 0.9 ± 1.2; p = 0.033) and at 12 months (0.1 ± 0.2 vs. 0.5 ± 0.7; p = 0.002). The reported KOOS score was higher in the PEMF group at 6 months (83.0 ± 10.0 vs. 78.0 ± 14.0; p = 0.048) and 12 months (90.0 ± 7.0 vs. 85.0 ± 10.0; p = 0.009), and SF-12 physical component summary was higher at 6 months.
CONCLUSION: PEMF therapy, used as an adjunct to standard perioperative care, was associated with lower pain scores and better selected patient-reported outcomes after ACL-R in patients with concomitant BB. The clinical findings support PEMF therapy as a promising noninvasive strategy to improve early recovery after ACL-R.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I.

title: Trustworthy AI for multimodal load-response modelling in team sports: a scoping review and full-text validation audit.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Artificial intelligence (AI), machine-learning and conventional statistical prediction methods are increasingly used in team-sport athlete monitoring, but it remains unclear whether current studies are validated and reported in ways that support trustworthy prospective use. This scoping review mapped predictive-modelling studies in team-sport athlete monitoring and multimodal load-response modelling and audited their validation and reporting practices.
METHODS: Searches were conducted in OpenAlex, PubMed, Scopus and SPORTDiscus for records published from 2010 to 2026. After deduplication, screening and updated OpenAlex rerun screening, 258 studies were included and audited from full text. Systematic duplicate screening was not performed; full-text eligibility assessment and original audit coding were completed by a single reviewer. Data were extracted on publication characteristics, sport context, data modalities, modelled outcomes, model families and validation practices. A 10-domain trustworthy-AI audit assessed prediction context, temporal validity, repeated-observation independence, external validation, leakage control, calibration, class-imbalance handling, interpretability, uncertainty reporting and deployment/actionability. Bibliometric and NLP analyses provided complementary field mapping. A second reviewer independently assessed 45 studies from the original 223-study audit subset across all ten audit domains.
RESULTS: The literature expanded rapidly after 2021, with performance modelling and injury-risk prediction as the dominant applications. Studies frequently used GPS/GNSS, session-RPE/internal load, wellness/sleep, HR/HRV, neuromuscular testing, IMU/accelerometry and video-derived features. Random forests, logistic/linear models and gradient boosting were the most common model families. Deployment-relevant validation remained limited. After targeted reassessment and updated-search incorporation, temporal validity was strongly documented in 28 studies (10.9%), while independent external validation was strongly documented in one study (0.4%) and partially documented in one additional study (0.4%). Leakage control, calibration, repeated-observation independence and model-level uncertainty reporting were also uncommon. Pre-correction exact agreement in the independent audit subset was 65.3% overall and varied substantially across domains.
DISCUSSION: Predictive modelling in team-sport athlete monitoring is expanding, but model development has advanced faster than trustworthy validation practice. Future studies should define the intended decision context, preserve temporal and player-level data structure, prevent leakage, report calibration and uncertainty, validate models under realistic deployment conditions and translate outputs into practitioner-facing decision support.

title: Train hard, recover smart: the supplement framework to enhance exercise recovery in recreational and elite-level athletes.
abstract: Background: Exercise-induced inflammation and muscle damage are frequent consequences of structured physical activity that facilitate muscle growth and subsequent training adaptations. Performance improvements are strongly dependent upon athletes' capacity to successfully recover from previous sessions or challenging efforts, particularly when opportunities to rest and recover are limited. Nutritional practices centered around acute or chronic ingestion of certain foods or dietary bioactive compounds have been shown to accelerate neurophysiological and subjective recovery outcomes and may be worthy of consideration in both recreationally active and professional athletic populations. Methods: This review provides a comprehensive summary of dietary strategies to promote exercise recovery that are supported by robust scientific evidence, including systematic reviews, randomized clinical trials, and observational studies up to August 2025. Results: Despite substantial variability in evidence quality, identified nutrients, dietary supplements, and bioactive compounds of greatest interest for athletes are omega-3 fatty acids and creatine monohydrate, while additional compounds showing promising results in improving subjective or objective recovery metrics such as inflammatory biomarkers, muscle soreness, and fatigue include magnesium, taurine, curcumin, L-Carnitine, Ashwagandha, anthocyanins, L-Citrulline, gingerol, tart cherry, beetroot, and pomegranate juice. Nutrients or compounds often popularized but requiring further investigation, current research gaps, and methodological limitations within the available body of literature are also discussed. Conclusion: The findings outlined in this review may inform evidence-based recovery nutrition strategies for both elite and recreational athletes.

title: Monitoring External Load and Internal Responses Across Selected Endurance Sports: A Scoping Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Endurance-sport monitoring combines external-load measures with physiological and subjective responses, but studies vary in their measurement techniques, interpretation, and links to action. This scoping review mapped how these indicators have been studied and the types of evidence linking them to training and athlete outcomes.
METHODS: PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched on 24 October 2026. Eligible original research evaluated at least one non-invasive indicator on at least two days during a documented training period or endurance exposure of seven days or longer in six selected endurance sports. Age eligibility was a sample mean/median of at least 18 years or explicit adult recruitment. Findings were summarized descriptively without meta-analysis or formal critical appraisal.
RESULTS: Of 8398 screened records, 83 database-derived reports and six reports from other methods were assessed in full, and 56 reports were included. Of these, 15 reports concerned training-load quantification, 32 examined autonomic or physiological responses, and 9 studied subjective responses. By evidence type, 13 examined measurement properties or response behavior, 20 considered concurrent or longitudinal associations, 12 assessed prospective relationships, and 11 examined monitoring-informed action rules. Relationships varied with calibration, measurement protocol, time window, sport, and outcome.
CONCLUSIONS: The mapped comparisons do not establish broad transferable action thresholds or comparative effectiveness. Future research should evaluate explicit monitoring-and-action rules against adaptations, performance, and health outcomes.

title: Education and exercise compared to education alone for hip osteoarthritis: Protocol for the EDUEX randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patient education (EDU) and exercise are universally recommended as first-line treatment for hip and knee osteoarthritis (OA). Specifically in hip OA, the evidence that exercise is a necessary addition when comprehensive EDU is delivered is sparse. Additionally, no randomized trial has evaluated effects of exercise on articular cartilage in hip OA assessed by magnetic resonance imaging. This randomized trial will evaluate whether adding progressive resistance training (PRT) to EDU results in superior improvements in 1) patient-reported physical function and 2) collagen integrity of the hip articular cartilage.
METHODS: This multicenter, stratified, block randomized, controlled, parallel-group, efficacy, superiority trial will be conducted at hospitals and physiotherapy clinics in Denmark. A total of 150 people with hip OA will be enrolled and randomized in a 1:1 ratio to only participate in an EDU program or to the same EDU program and additionally 12 months of partly supervised group-based PRT. The primary outcome is between-group difference in change from baseline to 12 months in 1) the Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score activities of daily living function subscale for the primary clinical superiority study and 2) T2 relaxation time mapping of the hip articular cartilage for the primary mechanistic superiority study (P-MECH).
DISCUSSION: The EDUEX trial will provide high-quality evidence for assessing the clinical efficacy of adding PRT to EDU in people with hip OA while also assessing the effects on hip articular cartilage.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT06391554.

title: Paraspinal Muscle Quality and Functional Outcomes Following Lumbar Fusion: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Lumbar interbody fusion (LIF) procedures are associated with postoperative paraspinal muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration (FI), which may influence long-term pain and functional recovery. However, the relationship between muscle quality, both pre- and postoperatively, and patient-reported outcomes remains unclear for patients undergoing lumbar fusion. This correlation was compared between minimally invasive surgery (MIS) and conventional open surgery (COS) approaches to assess differences in postoperative muscle preservation and functional outcomes.
METHODS: A systematic review, conducted following PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420250650064), examined studies found in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science through February 2025. Studies were included if they assessed adult patients undergoing LIF with preoperative CT or MRI evaluation of the multifidus (MF) or erector spinae (ES) and reported postoperative cross-sectional area (CSA), FI, or patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs).
RESULTS: Twenty studies met inclusion criteria; risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I for 19 non-randomized studies and RoB 2 for one randomized trial. Seven of nine COS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, including all three COS-only studies, measured by CSA and FI. Two of twelve MIS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, with four of six direct comparisons found smaller declines in CSA, increases in FI, or both after MIS compared to COS in at least one muscle or setting. Higher preoperative muscle quality, particularly lower FI, and smaller pre- to postoperative muscle changes were associated with greater PROM improvements. Across the PROM-focused studies, four of the five reported that higher preoperative CSA or lower FI predicted better postoperative improvements in functional outcomes, with one identifying that MF FI of 61% or greater as a threshold for failing to achieve clinically meaningful ODI improvements.
CONCLUSION: MIS techniques were associated with a decrease in pre- to postoperative FI compared with COS, although PROM improvement occurred across both approaches. While preoperative paraspinal muscle quality and size decreases are generally smaller with better functional outcomes following postoperative LIF, this relationship is not consistently observed across all studies or surgical techniques. These findings suggest that the current imaging-based biomarkers may not fully capture the multifactorial nature of functional recovery and underscore the need for further research into additional predictors of muscle recovery.

title: Diagnosis, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport after Athletic Hamstring Injury: An ICCUS Society Consensus Statement.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athletic hamstring injuries (AHSI) remain a persistent challenge because recurrence is common and clinical decisions often depend on incomplete evidence. This consensus statement is intended to give clinicians a practical, unified framework for classification, rehabilitation, and return to sport after athletic hamstring injury. The purpose of this study was to achieve expert consensus on the management of athletic hamstring injuries through a structured, scientific survey approach.
STUDY DESIGN: Delphi Survey.
METHODS: A modified Delphi process, aligned with CREDES guidelines, was conducted with an expert panel of sports physical therapists identified as having specific expertise in AHSI from the ICCUS Society. Consensus was defined a priori as at least 80% agreement or disagreement on a 5-point Likert scale. Statements addressed three areas: AHSI examination and classification, rehabilitation and management, and return to sport (RTS) testing.
RESULTS: Sixty statements were developed across three domains. Seventeen experienced clinicians completed the final round. Overall, 54 statements reached consensus, with a mean Likert score of 4.56 ± 0.37 out of 5 (strongly agree), and mean agreement of 89.88% ± 12.1%. Experts supported standardized terminology, MRI and the use of diagnostic ultrasound for diagnosis when appropriate, individualized and criterion-based rehabilitation, progressive tissue loading and length restoration, early neuromuscular control, gradual running and agility progression, progression to pain-free sprinting, objective strength assessment, sport-specific workloads, and athlete readiness as key RTS criteria.
DISCUSSION: The findings emphasize active rehabilitation guided by measurable progress rather than reliance on fixed thresholds. Clinicians should combine injury classification, functional presentation, symptom response, objective testing, sport demands, and athlete confidence when advancing rehabilitation and making RTS decisions.
CONCLUSION: This ICCUS Society consensus statement offers a practical roadmap for managing AHSI: classify clearly, load progressively, monitor symptoms, test objectively, and return athletes only when sport-specific running, sprinting, strength, training tolerance, and readiness align.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 4.

title: Low energy availability in recreational high-intensity functional training athletes: associations with health and performance outcomes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Low energy availability (LEA) is the primary etiological factor underlying Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S), yet limited research has examined LEA risk and associated health and performance outcomes in recreational high-intensity functional training (HIFT) athletes. The purpose of this study was to evaluate energy availability (EA) and physiological outcomes aligned with the RED-S Health and Performance Models in a recreational HIFT cohort.
METHODS: Thirty participants (females: n = 18, males: n = 12; 31.2 ± 8.2 years) completed a two-week prospective observational study with repeated measures of energy intake, exercise energy expenditure, and associated health and performance-related measures. Energy intake was assessed via dietary logs, exercise energy expenditure was estimated using a wearable armband, and EA was calculated relative to dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry-derived fat-free mass. Participants were classified as LEA if EA was <30 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1. Performance-related outcomes included rating of perceived exertion (RPE), perceived recovery status (PRS), and total quality recovery (TQR). Health-related outcomes included sleep duration, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and bone mineral density (BMD) (reported by Z-Score).
RESULTS: Mean EA was 24.9 ± 9.7 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1, with 80% (n = 24) of participants demonstrating EA below the LEA classification threshold. The high prevalence of LEA should be interpreted cautiously given the potential for underreporting dietary intake. LEA status was not associated with differences in recovery, sleep quality, or BMD (p > 0.05), and EA was not significantly correlated with performance or health outcomes. In an exploratory analysis, sleep duration was moderately positively associated with TQR (ρ = 0.46, p = 0.01); however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously given the number of comparisons performed.
DISCUSSION: Despite the high prevalence of LEA, associated health and performance impairments were not detected, suggesting that measurable consequences of LEA may not be evident over a short observation period in recreational HIFT athletes. These findings support ongoing monitoring of EA, fueling practices, and recovery behaviors to reduce the potential long-term consequences associated with RED-S.
