title: Sex- and Sport-Specific Differences in Mobility and Muscle Function Characteristics in Division I Athletes.
abstract: Gonzalez, AM, Sell, KM, Mangine, GT, Ghigiarelli, JJ, Gerland, RW, Deveaux, B, DiMonda, R, Prendergast, JM, and Bentivegna, J. Sex- and sport-specific differences in mobility and muscle function characteristics in Division I athletes. J Strength Cond Res 40(12): 1569-1580, 2026-The purpose of the present investigation was to compare sex- and sport-specific differences in joint mobility, bilateral asymmetry, and muscle function characteristics among Division I collegiate athletes. Two hundred and seventy six male (n = 144) and female (n = 132) athletes from 7 sports completed a comprehensive, preseason assessment battery. Mobility assessments included hip, shoulder, ankle, thoracic, and pelvic range-of-motion, as well as sit-and-reach performance. Muscle function assessments included measures of vertical jump height, hand grip strength, and hip abduction/adduction strength. Measures were analyzed using mixed-model analyses of variance to examine effects of sex, sport, and limb dominance. Clear sex- and sport-specific differences were observed across multiple mobility measures. Female athletes demonstrated significantly greater joint mobility than male athletes across several anatomical regions (p < 0.001-0.03; η2p = 0.02-0.16), whereas male athletes display superior muscle function performance across strength (p < 0.001-0.02; η2p = 0.06-0.3) and vertical jump (p < 0.001, η2p = 0.50) measures. Mobility asymmetries varied substantially by sport and joint, while strength asymmetries were minimal across groups. These findings provide sex- and sport-specific reference data and reinforce the importance of individualized interpretation of mobility and muscle function assessments in athletic populations.

title: Age- and maturation-related differences in the relationships between sport-specific agility, linear sprint, and vertical jump performance in young male soccer players.
abstract: Agility shows weaker associations with physical qualities in older compared with younger age groups of young athletes; however, these relationships have not yet been examined using ecologically valid agility tests. The aim of this study was to assess the age- and maturation-related differences in the relationships between agility, linear sprint, and vertical jump performance in young male soccer players, using an agility test with a soccer-specific human stimulus. Fifty-seven young male soccer players participated in the study, divided into two groups based on chronological age (U11/12 and U13/14) and estimated maturity status (Pre-PHV and Circa-PHV). Participants completed linear sprint tests (10-m, 20-m), a countermovement jump test (CMJ), and a soccer-specific human stimulus-based agility test. Significant correlations were observed between agility and 10-m (ρ = 0.468, P = 0.030; ρ = 0.386, P = 0.020) and 20-m sprint performance (ρ = 0.502, P = 0.021; ρ = 0.450, P = 0.006) in the U11/12 and Pre-PHV groups, respectively, whereas these correlations were nonsignificant in the U13/14 and Circa-PHV groups. However, formal comparisons revealed no significant differences in correlation magnitude between chronological age or maturity groups (P > 0.05). Nonsignificant correlations were found between agility and CMJ performance in all subgroups. Partial correlation analyses controlling for maturity offset attenuated all the observed associations in the total sample and in all subgroups. Overall, agility showed generally limited associations with linear sprint and vertical jump performance, with no evidence that the strength of these relationships differed systematically across the examined age or maturity groups.

title: Nationwide Trends, Regional Variation and Seasonality of Surgically Treated Achilles Tendon Rupture in Japan: An Analysis of Descriptive Epidemiological Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Achilles tendon rupture (ATR) is a common foot and ankle injury among physically active adults. Nationwide evidence on long-term trends, regional variation, seasonality and COVID-19-related changes in Japan is limited. We characterised the surgical burden of ATR using a national administrative database.
METHODS: We conducted a nationwide descriptive epidemiological study using aggregated data from the National Database of Health Insurance Claims and Specific Health Checkups (NDB) Open Data for fiscal years (FY) 2014-2022. Temporal trends, prefectural variation, seasonal patterns and pandemic-associated changes were examined using counts, population-based rates and quasi-Poisson regression.
RESULTS: During FY2014-2019, approximately 11,200 surgeries were performed annually (8.8 per 100,000 person). In FY2020, incidence declined to 5.9 per 100,000 (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0.67), with greater reductions among adults aged 30-59 (61%-64% of baseline) and, after age adjustment, among women (IRR 0.61 vs. 0.71 in men; interaction p = 0.039). Incidence partially recovered in FY2021-2022 (7.6 per 100,000; IRR 0.86). Incidence varied across the 47 prefectures (pre-COVID range: 5.0-16.7 per 100,000), and all declined in FY2020 (mean ratio 0.69). Monthly counts peaked in spring-early summer and were higher in spring than in winter (p = 0.018).
CONCLUSIONS: The incidence of surgically treated ATR in Japan was stable before the COVID-19 pandemic, declined markedly in FY2020 and partially recovered thereafter, with the largest reductions among working-age adults and women. Regional variation and seasonality were preserved. These findings can inform surgical and rehabilitation service planning.

title: Time-Efficient Reactive Agility Training Improves Motor and Cognitive Components of Reactive Agility in Open- and Closed-Skill Athletes: A 6-Week Intervention Study.
abstract: Reactive agility (RA), the ability to respond to external stimuli with whole-body movements as quickly and precisely as possible, is crucial for many sports, particularly open-skill sports, and is influenced by both motor and cognitive abilities. This study aims to investigate which of the underlying components of RA is most improved through RA training, whether prior experience with RA movements influences the rate of improvement, and whether a time-ecological approach also leads to improvements. Assessments included 19 open-skill and 26 closed-skill athletes with different competitive backgrounds. RA training was carried out once a week for six weeks with each session lasting 20 minutes. Pre- and post-assessments were conducted for RA (Random Star Run), change-of-direction (t-Test), and cognitive performance (Stroop test). Baseline differences between open- and closed-skill athletes and performance level were evaluated using 2 × 2 ANOVA. Intervention effects were calculated using repeated measures ANOVA. Open-skill athletes were significantly faster within the RA task than closed-skill athletes (p = 0.017; F = 6.247; η2 p = 0.132). Both groups improved significantly across all outcome measures (p < 0.05; RA and both underlying properties) with no interaction effects of group × time (p > 0.05). One weekly 20-min training session is sufficient to improve RA, and selected motor and cognitive performance parameters. Prior experience, based on regular participation in open-skill sports, seems to be associated with higher RA performance but does not moderate training adaptations, as both groups improved similarly in RA and the underlying motor and cognitive functions.

title: Mechanisms and Movement Patterns of Ankle Sprain Injuries in Male Handball: A Video-Based Analysis.
abstract: Ankle sprains are among the most common injuries in handball. However, evidence on high-risk movements and injury circumstances is scarce. This video analysis study investigated the situational characteristics of athletes sustaining ankle sprains. A systematic web search (YouTube, Google News) identifying video recordings of ankle injuries in male handball players was performed. Two independent examiners extracted sample information (e.g., age, height, weight, position), mechanism of injury (direct, indirect, non-contact), movement pattern (landing, change of direction/CoD, running, shuffle, step/lunge, other), action speed, focus of visual attention, and time of injury. In addition to descriptive statistics, χ2-tests were used to examine variable associations. A total of 118 video-recorded injuries were obtained. Most sprains were direct contact injuries (n = 72, 61.0%), and the most frequent movement patterns were landing (n = 46), running (n = 15), step/lunge (n = 14), and CoD (n = 13). While direct injuries occurred primarily during landing (43%), non-contact mechanisms (85%) were, by far, the main cause of injury during change of Direction movements (p < 0.01). In the majority of cases, movement speed was moderate (n = 63) and visual attention was directed to the ball (n = 56). Landings are the most frequent cause of ankle sprains in male handball players. Although the largest share, particularly landing-related injuries, results from direct contact, non-contact sprains display a unique pattern as they mostly occur during CoD. Conditioning coaches and health personnel may consider this disparity when designing preventive measures.

title: Age-related slowing of sensorimotor reaction time in masters track and field athletes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Masters athletes offer a powerful model for understanding how lifelong training shapes age‑related changes in reaction time (RT), a key indicator of sensorimotor performance.
PURPOSE: This cross-sectional study examined RT in masters track and field athletes across age, sex, RT tasks of varying complexity, and event disciplines (endurance, power, sprint).
METHODS: A total of 182 competitors (82 females) from the 2025 World Masters Athletics Championships completed four RT tasks using a wireless light-based testing system.
RESULTS: RT increased progressively with age across all tasks, with the slowest responses consistently observed in athletes ≥80 years old. Female athletes demonstrated slower RT than males, and RT increased systematically with task complexity. Sprint athletes showed faster RT than endurance athletes overall, although event‑specific differences did not persist within age groups. Age was positively associated with RT in all tasks (r = 0.41-0.53), with similar correlation strengths between sexes. Quadratic age effects emerged selectively in male athletes for two-hand simple and step-choice tasks, suggesting accelerated slowing at older ages in tasks requiring greater motor coordination. Linear regression models indicated that RT increased by approximately 3.3-3.6 ms per year of age after adjusting for sex, task, and event discipline, while body composition variables were not significant predictors.
CONCLUSIONS: Although lifelong training is associated with better sensorimotor performance, slower RT remains evident in masters athletes, with consistent sex differences and minimal influence of event discipline.

title: Immediate Return or Overnight Stay? Sleep Responses by Postmatch Travel Strategy and Match Participation in Professional Football.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Late European away fixtures can disrupt sleep, but the influence of immediate return versus overnight stay, and whether responses differ by match participation, remains unclear.
HYPOTHESIS: Postmatch travel strategy would influence sleep quality and duration across the prematch, match, and subsequent nights, with responses moderated by match participation.
STUDY DESIGN: Observational repeated-measures field study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: A total of 19 outfield English Premier League players were monitored across 10 European away fixtures (5 immediate return and 5 overnight stay). Self-reported sleep quality (1 to 7) and sleep duration were recorded on the prematch, match, and subsequent nights. Fixed-effects models examined condition, time, and match participation, with standard errors clustered by player.
RESULTS: Sleep quality was lower than prematch baseline on the match and subsequent nights (both β = -0.62 arbitrary units [AU]; P < 0.01; g = -0.63). After overnight stay, sleep quality improved from the match to the subsequent night in players who participated and those who did not (β = 0.69 and 0.63 AU; 95% CIs, 0.37-0.90 and 0.47-0.91; P < 0.01), whereas no change occurred after immediate return. Across participation groups, sleep duration was lower after overnight stay than immediate return on the match night (β = -1.94 hours; P < 0.01; g = -1.26) and subsequent night (β = -1.02 hours; P = 0.02; g = -0.67). However, after overnight stay, sleep duration increased between these nights by 1.45 hours in participants and 1.43 hours in nonparticipants (P < 0.01), with no significant change after immediate return. Participation moderated sleep duration on both postfixture nights (β = 1.27 and 1.64 hours; P ≤ 0.04; g = 0.82 and 1.07).
CONCLUSION: Neither travel strategy was uniformly superior. Overnight stay was associated with poorer absolute sleep duration but a clearer next-night rebound in sleep quality and duration.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Postmatch travel should be planned case by case, considering itinerary, next-day demands, and individual match exposure rather than applying a single team-wide policy.

title: The Relationship Between Muscle Strength and Jump Height with Bone Mineral Density (BMD) in Elite Female Soccer Players: The Mediating Role of Lean Body Mass.
abstract: Soccer is one of the most widely practiced and studied sports worldwide. The increasing professionalization of women's soccer has raised interest in bone health. This study aimed to analyze the mediating role of lean body mass in the association between muscle strength, jump height, and bone mineral density (BMD) in elite female soccer players. A cross-sectional study was conducted with 28 players from the Spanish national soccer team. Muscle strength was assessed using estimated 1RM in the deadlift, jump height through the countermovement jump (CMJ) test, and BMD using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Lean body mass exhibited a significant indirect effect on the association between muscle strength and BMD at the lumbar spine (β = 0.2848, B = 0.0020, 95% CI for B [0.0001-0.0049]), femoral neck (β = 0.2562, B = 0.0020, 95% CI for B [0.0003-0.0052]), and whole body (β = 0.3769, B = 0.0019, 95% CI for B [0.0005-0.0038]). These results suggest that muscle strength alone may not fully explain inter-individual differences in bone mass and that lean body mass may play an important role in this relationship. Combining soccer training with targeted strength training could help maximize peak bone mass and mitigate future bone loss in these female athletes. Longitudinal studies are needed to confirm these findings.

title: Initial Findings on the Physiological Effects of Flotation Restricted Environmental Stimulation Therapy on Muscle Oxygenation and Heart Rate Variability in University-Aged Concussed and Healthy Athletes.
abstract: Flotation restricted environmental stimulation therapy (flotation-REST) activates pathways consistent with increased cardiac vagal modulation and parasympathetic influence that may promote rapid autonomic relaxation. While previous studies have explored its psychological benefits, little is known about the physiological effects, particularly in athletes recovering from mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). This study investigates the acute and longitudinal effects of flotation-REST on muscle oxygenation (MO2) and heart rate variability (HRV) in healthy and mTBI athletes. Thirteen healthy and six mTBI athletes completed one hour flotation-REST sessions across ten weeks. Vastus lateralis MO2 was measured using near-infrared spectroscopy, and HRV (mean R-R interval, SDNN, heart rate) was assessed using chest strap monitors and analyzed using Kubios. Pre- and post-flotation-REST measurements were taken in both supine and standing positions. Significance was set at p < 0.05. A linear mixed-effects model underlined an acute increase pre-to-post flotation-REST for MO2 (p < .001) and mean R-R interval (p = .003), with significant Time × Position interactions for both (p < .001 and p = .040, respectively). Mean heart rate also decreased significantly (p = .022), whereas SDNN showed no change. Longitudinally, a significant improvement across the sessions was observed for MO2 (p = .022), mean R-R interval (p < .001), and mean heart rate (p = .001), but not SDNN. A significant Session × Position interaction was observed for SDNN (p = .016). No significant Session × Group or Session × Time interactions were observed for the HRV parameters. Flotation-REST may be a promising recuperation technique for post-mTBI athletes who cannot participate in traditional recovery strategies. These findings suggest that flotation-REST may be associated with both acute physiological responses and changes across repeated sessions, although the underlying mechanisms remain to be determined.

title: Body recomposition in adults: mechanisms, modulators, and practical algorithms for simultaneous skeletal muscle mass gain and fat mass loss.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Body recomposition is the concurrent increase in fat-free mass (FFM) or skeletal muscle mass and decrease in fat mass (FM) within the same intervention period. Although hypertrophy is commonly pursued in energy surplus and FM loss in energy deficit, controlled trials indicate that recomposition can occur when progressive resistance training (PRT), adequate protein intake, and an appropriate energy prescription are combined.
METHODS: We conducted a structured narrative review of randomised trials, meta-analyses, and selected mechanistic studies in adults, with emphasis on FFM, FM, strength, and performance outcomes. Device heterogeneity was considered when interpreting evidence, with greatest weight placed on four-compartment and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) outcomes.
RESULTS: PRT combined with higher protein intake, typically ~1.6-2.4 g/kg/day and higher relative intakes during energy restriction or leanness, is the most consistent strategy for recomposition. Effects are largest in untrained individuals and those with higher adiposity, smaller in trained or lean athletes, and still feasible in older adults when anabolic resistance is addressed with supervised PRT and sufficient protein. Moderate deficits, carbohydrate allocation around key sessions, sleep, and recovery support FFM retention or accretion while facilitating FM loss. Practical applications: Programmes should pair progressive overload with protein-centred diets, modest energy deficits, and periodic monitoring of body composition and performance.
CONCLUSIONS: Body recomposition is feasible but context-dependent; expected changes are generally modest in trained or lean populations and require individualised adjustment.

title: Early Bilateral Periprosthetic Femoral Fractures After One-Stage Bilateral Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Rare Case Report With Literature Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Periprosthetic femoral fractures (PFFs) following total knee arthroplasty (TKA) are uncommon but potentially devastating complications. Early bilateral PFFs occurring shortly after one-stage bilateral TKA are extremely rare and pose significant challenges in diagnosis and management.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 62-year-old woman underwent one-stage bilateral posterior-stabilized (PS) TKA for advanced knee osteoarthritis. Three weeks postoperatively, she sustained bilateral supracondylar femoral fractures following a minor sprain. Radiographic evaluation confirmed bilateral distal PFFs classified as Lewis-Rorabeck type IIA, with stable femoral components. The patient had multiple risk factors, including long-standing diabetes mellitus, osteoporosis, and hypoalbuminemia. One-stage bilateral open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) with locking plates combined with autogenous iliac bone grafting was performed after comprehensive preoperative assessment. Postoperatively, the patient achieved satisfactory fracture healing and functional recovery. At 1-year follow-up, radiographs demonstrated complete union, the patient was pain-free, knee range of motion was 0°-100° bilaterally, and the Hospital for Special Surgery (HSS) score was 90.
CONCLUSIONS: Early bilateral PFFs can occur after TKA even following minor trauma. Patient-related factors, such as diabetes mellitus and osteoporosis, may increase susceptibility to fracture. Intraoperative microdamage, femoral impaction, and early mechanical loading have been proposed as potential contributing factors; however, their roles in the present cases remain speculative and cannot be confirmed based on the available evidence. Careful surgical technique, individualized postoperative rehabilitation, and early identification of patients at increased fracture risk may help reduce the likelihood of this rare complication.

title: Adhesive and Antibacterial Bio-Based Hydrogel for Human Voice Recognition and Osteoarthritis Recovery Monitoring.
abstract: Conductive hydrogels derived from natural polysaccharides hold great promise for next generation wearable electronics owing to their intrinsic biocompatibility, adhesiveness, and tunable mechanical properties. However, realizing amylum-based hydrogels with simultaneously high stretchability, sensitivity, strong adhesion and antibacterial performance remains a significant challenge. Herein, a multifunctional ionic hydrogel, marked as PAPC4 hydrogel, composed of polyacrylamide (PAAm), amylum and phenol-modified chitosan is developed via a one-pot synthesis strategy. The hydrogel exhibits exceptional stretchability (up to 1605%), short response time (16.1 ms), high optical transparency (96%), strong adhesion (43.2 kPa on PVC) and pronounced antibacterial activity. Cytotoxicity assays, live/dead staining, and subcutaneous implantation supported its biocompatibility under the tested conditions, while bacterial assays demonstrated activity against Escherichia coli. As a strain sensor, PAPC4 detected joint movements and throat vibrations during speech. It also recorded differences in knee movement among control, osteoarthritis, and treated osteoarthritis groups in rats. These results support the use of this chitosan-starch composite hydrogel in wearable motion sensing and rehabilitation monitoring.

title: Tendon Reconstruction in the Red-Red Zone at 10 mm Provides Favorable Biomechanical Stability for Medial Meniscus Posterior Root Tears: A Porcine Biomechanical Study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To determine the optimal reconstruction zone and distance for tendon reconstruction of medial meniscus posterior root tears based on biomechanical performance.
METHODS: Thirty-six porcine knees with standardized medial meniscus posterior root tears underwent tendon reconstruction and were allocated to reconstruction in the red-red zone (Group A) or red-white zone (Group B). Each group was subdivided by reconstruction distance (5, 10, and 15 mm; n = 6 each). Constructs underwent cyclic loading (10-30 N, 1000 cycles), followed by load-to-failure testing. Cyclic displacement, ultimate failure load, elongation, stiffness, and failure modes were recorded.
RESULTS: Group A revealed smaller cyclic displacement than Group B after 1000 cycles (2.81 ± 0.16 vs 3.21 ± 0.13 mm; P < .001) and a higher ultimate failure load (291.04 ± 90.59 vs 196.88 ± 41.47 N; P < .001), whereas no between-group differences were observed in elongation (P = .975) or stiffness (P = .429). Regarding reconstruction distance, ultimate failure load in Group A was lower at 5 mm than at 10 and 15 mm (190.48 ± 51.51 N vs 344.90 ± 68.89 N and 337.73 ± 47.45 N, respectively; P < .001), whereas no significant differences were observed among distance subgroups in Group B (P = .390). In both groups, elongation was greater, and stiffness was lower at 5 mm than at 10 and 15 mm (all P < .028). A significant zone-distance interaction was observed for failure load (P < .001). All specimens failed by tendon cut-through.
CONCLUSIONS: Reconstruction in the red-red zone provides greater biomechanical stability than reconstruction in the red-white zone, and a 10-mm reconstruction distance offers greater strength than 5 mm with no additional biomechanical benefit at 15 mm.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings provide biomechanical guidance for optimizing tendon reconstruction strategies for medial meniscus posterior root tears.

title: Acute Circulating Responses and Four-Week Adaptations to Blood Flow-Restricted Resistance Training at Two Individualized Pressures in Male Sprinters.
abstract: Background: Acute metabolic responses to individualized blood flow restriction pressures remain incompletely characterized in trained athletes. Methods: Twenty-four male sprinters were randomized to blood flow-restricted resistance training (BFR-RT) at 50% or 80% of individual venous occlusion pressure (VOP; n = 12 each). Biochemical and untargeted plasma metabolomic responses were assessed before and after the first BFR-RT session. Strength, muscle morphology, and jump performance were assessed before and after four weeks. Results: Both groups showed acute lactate and growth hormone increases and cortisol decreases. Acute between-pressure biochemical differences did not remain significant after multiple-testing correction. Exploratory metabolomics identified shared candidate response patterns with differing mean amplitudes between pressures. Back-squat strength increased in both groups, while most functional changes showed no detected between-pressure difference. Conclusions: Both VOP prescriptions were accompanied by short-term strength gains. Candidate metabolic patterns characterized variation in the acute circulating response under the two pressure conditions.

title: A scoping review evaluating artificial intelligence applications across various injury prevention domains.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly utilized for injury prevention across diverse clinical and community settings including machine learning (ML). This scoping review aimed to synthesize the current literature on the applications and predictive performance of AI across multiple injury prevention domains.
METHODS: This scoping review searched five major databases, including PubMed, Embase, ScienceDirect, ProQuest, and the Cochrane Library, to identify studies evaluating AI applications for injury prevention published through May 2026. Eligible studies included original U.S.-based, English-language research across self-harm and suicide, abuse and violence, fall prevention, and sports injury prediction. Studies were excluded if they lacked measurable prevention outcomes or sufficient methodological detail, or focused on injury treatment rather than prevention, to ensure relevant and interpretable evidence for synthesis.
RESULTS: Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria. ML models generally outperformed or matched traditional screening methods for self-harm and suicide prediction (AUC 0.81-0.82), while multimodal approaches achieved the highest predictive accuracy (AUC 0.90). In abuse and violence prevention, AI predicted intimate partner violence with an AUC of 0.88 and identified cases before formal disclosure. AI also improved fall risk assessment by accurately categorizing patient risk levels, predicting future falls, and mitigating fall injuries through wearable airbag technology. ML models predicted future sports-related injuries (AUC 0.76-0.84), while identifying modifiable risk factors including workload, strength deficits, prior injury burden, and concussion history.
CONCLUSION: ML-based prediction showed promise for risk stratification in self-harm, suicide, intimate partner violence, and recurrent victimization. Additionally, AI predicted fall risk and identified athletes at risk for future sports-related injuries while detecting modifiable risk factors, including workload, prior injury burden, and strength deficits. Although these findings suggest that AI and ML may have potential applications in supporting earlier risk identification, informing targeted prevention strategies, and facilitating more personalized approaches to injury prevention, the limited available evidence warrants careful interpretation.

title: Beyond contact status: foot-ground movement transitions in ACL injury situations in young athletes.
abstract: Contact-based descriptions of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury may obscure the movement preceding injury. We retrospectively classified 151 ACL injury episodes in athletes aged 22 years or younger using questionnaires, clinical interviews, and available supplementary information. A second evaluator independently classified episodes. Foot-ground movement transitions involving deceleration or redirection were identified in 121 episodes (80.1%): 88 (72.7%) without preceding interpersonal contact and 33 (27.3%) following contact-related perturbation. Direct external contact accounted for 24 episodes (15.9%); contact roles were indeterminate in three (2.0%), and three (2.0%) represented other situations. Independent classifications agreed in 137/151 episodes (90.7%; Cohen's κ = 0.84). Identifiable foot-ground movement transitions occurred across conventional contact categories. This clinical perspective complements contact-based terminology without establishing a shared biomechanical ACL loading pathway.

title: Immediate effect of verbal cues on ACL injury relevant Knee loading during 180° and 90° cutting maneuvers in female university soccer and basketball athletes.
abstract: Young female athletes possess a high risk of rupturing their anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). High external peak knee abduction moments (pKAM) are a likely key risk factor for non-contact ACL injuries. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of performance-based movement feedback on pKAM during cutting maneuvers in female university athletes. Thirty-four female university soccer and basketball athletes completed preplanned 180° and 90° cutting trials while ground reaction forces and kinematics were simultaneously captured. Participants immediately received verbal cues targeting foot strike angle, foot progression angle, or trunk lean angle based on their performance. Athletes then repeated the trials post-feedback. Changes in pKAM between baseline and post-feedback trials were analyzed. Soccer and basketball athletes who received the FOOTstrike-angle cue significantly reduced pKAM for both cutting tasks (Soccer: 180°; -0.21 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 0.92; 90°; -0.28 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 1.16. Basketball: 180°; -0.07 Nm/kg, p = 0.02, d = 0.76; 90°; -0.30 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 0.82). The FOOTpro-angle cue significantly reduced pKAM during the 180° cut for soccer athletes (-0.10 Nm/kg, p = 0.01, d = 0.60), but not basketball. The TRUNKlean cue did not significantly affect pKAM for either sport. Individual feedback targeting forefoot landings and neutral foot progression angles can elicit immediate technique change and reduce ACL injury relevant knee loading during cutting maneuvers.

title: Scar Treatments in Hand Surgery.
abstract: Scar formation after hand surgery poses unique functional and aesthetic challenges because of the hand's complex anatomy, dense sensory innervation, and reliance on supple skin and tendon glide. Hypertrophic scars, keloids, adherent scars, and contractures can cause pain, hypersensitivity, restricted motion, and impaired activities of daily living, yet evidence guiding scar management in hand surgery remains limited and largely extrapolated from burn and general surgical populations. This review synthesizes current evidence on the biology, classification, prevention, and treatment of scars as they pertain to hand surgery. Nonoperative management, including silicone gel sheeting, compression therapy, intralesional corticosteroid injection, laser therapy, and hand therapy, forms the foundation of care. Operative interventions, ranging from scar excision and Z-plasty to skin grafting, local flap reconstruction, dermal substitutes, and tenolysis, address established contracture and adhesion when conservative measures fail. Emerging therapies, such as autologous fat grafting, growth factor modulation, platelet-rich plasma, and botulinum toxin A, show early promise but require validation in hand-specific trials. Optimal outcomes depend on a collaborative, individualized approach integrating patient risk stratification, meticulous surgical technique, and close coordination with hand therapy throughout the care continuum.

title: Arthroscopic Autologous Chondrocyte Implantation Using Specialized Instrumentation for Exposure, Preparation, and Delivery.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI) has been recognized as a leading option for treating large articular cartilage defects in the knee1,4. MACI (Vericel) is the current generation of ACI available for use in the United States and consists of autologous cultured chondrocytes seeded onto a resorbable type-I/III porcine collagen membrane4. For years, MACI implantation has required an arthrotomy in order to implant the membrane; however, in August 2024, the U.S. Food & Drug Administration (FDA) approved a supplemental Biologics License Application expanding the MACI label to include arthroscopic delivery to repair cartilage defects of the knee up to 4 cm2 in size. Arthroscopic delivery of the MACI implant represents a new approach that is less invasive. The present video article provides a step-by-step process for delivering the MACI membrane via an arthroscopic approach with use of specially designed MACI Arthro instruments (Vericel). Following proper preoperative planning, positioning, and surgical exposure, the arthroscopic technique involves defect preparation with curets and arthroscopic cutters, creation of a dry environment, and secure delivery of the cell-seeded membrane with use of a dedicated cannula and delivery system.
DESCRIPTION: The arthroscopic technique begins with preoperative planning, including portal selection to achieve a perpendicular approach to the lesion, which may be more straightforward for medial condylar defects and more challenging for lateral condylar lesions. After positioning and surgical exposure, a specialized arthroscopic instrument set, including cannulas, cutters, curets, and a delivery device, is utilized to measure and prepare the lesion. A dry arthroscopic field is established for membrane delivery, preferably without the use of a tourniquet. The chondrocyte-seeded membrane is trimmed to the exact size of the defect and is delivered into the defect with use of a dedicated delivery system. The graft is positioned and is secured with use of fibrin glue in the dry joint environment in order to ensure stability and integration. Rehabilitation follows the standard MACI protocol, despite the less-invasive arthroscopic approach, and has 4 stages based on the status of the graft (0 to 6 weeks, protection and motion; 6 to 12 weeks, transition and proliferation; 12 to 26 weeks, remodeling; >26 weeks, maturation). To optimize graft maturation, the recommended postoperative regimen is continuous passive motion for 3 weeks, followed by the use of a brace locked in extension while walking for 6 weeks, and then progressive physical therapy.
ALTERNATIVES: An alternative to the presently described procedure is the use of an open MACI technique.
RATIONALE: Arthroscopic MACI is less invasive than the use of an open MACI technique.
EXPECTED OUTCOMES: In a series of studies, research teams from the University of Western Australia evaluated arthroscopic delivery of the MACI membrane, introducing the membrane into the knee via a large-bore, valveless arthroscopic cannula. In a 12-month study, early outcomes of the technique were encouraging among the first 10 prospectively assessed patients. Patients reported less pain and better symptom scores per the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), as compared with previously reported open MACI outcomes4. In an additional 24-month study, outcomes in 20 patients further supported the feasibility and safety of the arthroscopic technique. Significant improvements were noted across all KOOS subscales postoperatively, although without a control group the true treatment effect could not be isolated. MRI findings also demonstrated progressive morphologic graft repair over 24 months, with 90% of patients showing good-to-excellent graft infill and 70% achieving a good-to-excellent overall MRI composite score at 24 months. These results indicate that the technique is safe and rfeasible, with improved clinical and radiographic outcomes over the 2-year follow-up period1. In a third study of the first 31 patients who underwent arthroscopic MACI, 93% reported being satisfied with their pain level postoperatively. Additionally, 90% reported being satisfied with improvements in their ability to undertake daily activities, and 80% had improvements in participating in sports. Graft infill significantly improved over time, with 90% of patients demonstrating good-to-excellent tissue infill at 5 years postoperatively. There were 2 graft failures (6%) at 5 years postoperatively. The authors concluded that arthroscopic MACI demonstrated strong clinical and radiographic outcomes with high patient satisfaction up to 5 years postoperatively2. A retrospective study comparing the arthroscopic technique to a mini-open approach demonstrated better active knee range of motion and strength and fewer postoperative complications with use of the arthroscopic approach3.
IMPORTANT TIPS: Ensure that the portal allows for a perpendicular approach to the defect.Place the cutting guide toward the edge of the membrane; this allows for additional membrane harvest if needed, as well as easy removal of the membrane once it has been cut.The membrane should be the same size as or slightly smaller (rather than slightly larger) than the articular cartilage defect; the MACI should cover the prepared defect without overhanging margins.
ACRONYMS AND ABBREVIATIONS: DVT = deep venous thrombosisMRI = magnetic resonance imaging.

title: Should Nerve Transfer Surgery be the Standard of Care for Cervical Spinal Cord Injury?
abstract: Nerve transfer surgery is a promising intervention to improve upper limb function following cervical spinal cord injury, but there are knowledge gaps about optimal candidates, surgical timing, rehabilitation, and outcomes. The purpose of this review is to provide a critical analysis of the literature for nerve transfer surgery in this population, while also emphasizing the difficulty in generating high-quality evidence in this field. We establish that the outcomes from nerve transfer are on aggregate positive, but the individual response can be variable. We also discuss several aspects that have not been previously considered: (1) peri-operative challenges such as the optimal timing of the intervention in a complicated clinical milieu; (2) the potential benefits of combining nerve and tendon transfer in the same limb; (3) how nerve transfer surgery may be affected by and how it can potentially improve spasticity. Finally, we will introduce newly characterized central and peripheral nerve system barriers to nerve transfer rehabilitation, which necessitate novel combinatorial approaches to optimize patient outcomes.

title: The impact of mindfulness on sleep, cognitive function and athletic performance of young males migrating to the plateau.
abstract:
AIMS: To examine whether an 8-week mindfulness training program was associated with changes in sleep quality, cognitive function, and athletic performance in young men who migrated to high-altitude regions.
METHODS: Ninety-six young male migrants were randomly assigned to an 8-week mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) program (n = 48) or a no-intervention control group (n = 48). Sleep quality (PSQI), cognitive processing (P300 latency), and athletic performance (3000-m run time) were assessed before and after the intervention.
RESULTS: The mindfulness group was associated with greater improvements in sleep quality (PSQI median: 7.5 to 5 vs. 8 to 8.5, P < 0.001) and cognitive processing speed (P300 latency median: 387 ms to 357 ms vs. 376.5 ms to 374.5 ms, P = 0.01) compared with controls. Exploratory analyses suggested that P300 amplitude increased in parietal and occipital regions. No significant between-group difference was observed in 3000-m run completion time (P = 0.51) or grade improvement rates (25.0% vs. 29.17%, P = 0.65).
CONCLUSION: An 8-week mindfulness intervention was associated with improved sleep quality and cognitive processing speed, but no significant association was observed with athletic performance, in young male migrants to high-altitude regions. These preliminary findings suggest potential benefits of mindfulness as a non-pharmacological strategy for high-altitude health management, pending replication with active control conditions.

title: Changes in energy availability, nutritional status, and physiological health across training phases in elite Chinese artistic swimmers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Low energy availability (LEA) adversely affects athletes'physiological health, yet studies in elite synchronized swimmers across different pre-competition training phases are scarce. This study evaluated changes in energy availability, nutritional status, and physiological health in Chinese elite female synchronized swimmers before the National Games.
METHODS: Ten Chinese elite female synchronized swimmers sequentially completed a 1-week tapering phase (TP) and a 4-week intensified training phase (ITP). At the end of each phase, dietary intake (weighed food records), exercise energy expenditure (heart rate monitoring), energy availability (EA), resting metabolic rate (RMR), body composition, and blood biomarkers were measured. Within each training phase, athletes were classified into LEA and non-LEA groups according to their EA levels, and between-group differences were compared. In addition, overall changes between TP and ITP were analyzed in the full cohort of 10 athletes.
RESULTS: LEA prevalence was 40% during the TP and 60% during the ITP. In unadjusted analyzes, the LEA group showed significantly lower EI (p = 0.025), VO₂ (p = 0.022), mRMR (p = 0.023), RMR ratio (p = 0.006), and intakes of carbohydrate (p = 0.023), protein (p = 0.015), fat (p = 0.032), calcium (p = 0.038), and iron (p = 0.044) during the TP, with large effect-size estimates. As expected from the classification criteria, EA was significantly lower in the LEA group during both the TP (p = 0.001) and ITP (p = 0.005). During the ITP, fat (p = 0.027) and zinc intakes (p = 0.036) were significantly lower in the LEA group, whereas carbohydrate and protein intakes were lower but did not reach statistical significance. In the overall cohort, EEE (p < 0.001) and T4 (p = 0.010) increased from TP to ITP, whereas ferritin (p = 0.012) and calcium intake (p = 0.007) decreased, with large effect-size estimates.
CONCLUSION: During intensified training, EEE increased without a corresponding increase in EI, suggesting that dietary intake may not have adequately matched the increased training demands and may have increased susceptibility to LEA. LEA was associated with lower energy and macronutrient intakes, potential calcium and iron inadequacies, and phase-specific reductions in RMR-related measures. Phase-related biomarker changes could not be attributed specifically to LEA. Individualized and periodized nutritional monitoring and intervention are recommended to better align energy and nutrient intake with training demands and support athlete health and performance.

title: Dysphagia as the Initial Manifestation of Anti-HMGCR Antibody-Positive Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy Complicated by Pulmonary Embolism.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (anti-HMGCR) antibody-positive immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) is a rare autoimmune myopathy characterized by progressive proximal muscle weakness and markedly elevated creatine kinase levels. Although commonly associated with prior statin exposure, statin-naïve cases and atypical presentations are well described. Patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies are also at increased risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE), though data specific to IMNM remain limited.
CASE PRESENTATION: An 83-year-old man with brief, remote statin exposure presented with progressive proximal muscle weakness and a three-year history of oropharyngeal dysphagia preceding limb involvement. Laboratory evaluation revealed markedly elevated creatine kinase and transaminases. Anti-HMGCR antibodies were positive, and muscle biopsy confirmed necrotizing myopathy. During evaluation for occult malignancy, bilateral pulmonary emboli were incidentally identified. The patient required high-dose corticosteroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and intravenous immunoglobulin for refractory disease. With aggressive immunosuppressive therapy and rehabilitation, he demonstrated substantial clinical recovery at 6 months.
CONCLUSION: This case highlights oropharyngeal dysphagia as an early and, for a prolonged period, isolated manifestation of anti-HMGCR antibody-positive IMNM; here, it preceded the onset of limb weakness by approximately 3 years. It underscores the importance of comprehensive diagnostic evaluation in patients with unexplained oropharyngeal dysfunction, in whom an inflammatory myopathy may otherwise be overlooked for years. Clinicians should maintain awareness of thrombotic risk in inflammatory myopathies, particularly during active disease. Early recognition and prompt immunosuppressive therapy remain critical to optimize outcomes and prevent irreversible muscle damage.

title: Vertical jump landing kinetics may be more sensitive to delayed-onset muscle soreness effects than forward and drop jumps.
abstract: Exercise-induced delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) may reduce joint range of motion and transiently impair muscle strength. However, DOMS-related symptoms do not consistently translate into measurable biomechanical changes in landing mechanics. Here we set out to determine whether exercise-induced DOMS alters landing kinetics in different landing tasks. Twenty-six physically active adults (15 women and 11 men) completed a squat protocol to induce lower extremity DOMS. Before and 48 h after the protocol, DOMS was assessed using a numerical pain rating scale, and the landing kinetics data were recorded during forward, vertical, and drop jumps. Joint stiffness and the joint contributions to the total support moment were determined and compared between baseline and DOMS conditions. DOMS significantly increased perceived muscle soreness and reduced vertical jump height by 16%. Joint stiffness did not differ between baseline and DOMS conditions for any landing task. Changes in total support moment (TSM) distribution were observed during vertical jump landings, with a reduced relative hip contribution at initial contact and an increased relative knee contribution at maximum knee flexion. No significant changes in TSM distribution were observed during forward or drop jump landings. These findings indicate that lower extremity DOMS may not necessarily alter overall landing stiffness but can modify inter-joint movement and torque strategies in vertical jump landing, highlighting the importance of evaluating movement mechanics alongside performance measures during recovery from strenuous exercise.

title: Genicular Artery Embolization for Knee Osteoarthritis: A Practical Guide and Future Directions on behalf of French Society of Rheumatology, Musculoskeletal Imaging Society, French Hip and Knee Society, French Society for Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery, French Society of Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine, and of French Society of Radiology.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To establish considerations for the indication and performance of genicular arteries embolization (GAE) for painful knee osteoarthritis on behalf of consortium of national societies.
METHODS: Based on literature review and clinical practice, a multidisciplinary group of 16 healthcare professionals including rheumatologists, interventional and MSK radiologists, physical and rehabilitation medicine physicians, knee orthopedic surgeons, and member of people living with OA association produced the considerations. Results : The group established 11 specific considerations. GAE is indicated for patients with painful knee osteoarthritis for whom no other cause of pain can be identified, and whose pain is refractory despite usual optimal medical treatment. A pre-therapeutic knee synovitis should be searched prior to GAE using a Doppler ultrasound or, even better, a contrast-enhanced MRI. Interventional radiologists should perform pre- and post-GAE consultations in collaboration with other musculoskeletal physician, in order to integrate GAE into the multimodal management strategy. Currently, there is no consensus on GAE techniques, and these should be individualized according to patient characteristics and interventional radiologist preferences. GAE may be repeated in selected cases. There are no contraindications to undergoing knee surgery after having GAE, but after a reasonable delay of three months. GAE may be considered in selected patients with persistent knee pain after knee replacement and after exclusion of other causes, including joint infection.
CONCLUSIONS: These considerations provide a structured guide for GAE in painful knee osteoarthritis. Several questions warrant further investigation through clinical or basic research.

title: Congenital Insensitivity to Pain With Anhidrosis Presenting as a Painful Destructive Lesion of the Proximal Tibia.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis (CIPA) is an NTRK1-related hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy that predisposes children to recurrent musculoskeletal injury and may mimic neoplastic or inflammatory bone disease.
METHODS: We report a 9-year-7-month-old girl with 3 months of right knee pain and swelling. Clinical examination, serial radiography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, histopathology, detailed autonomic history, whole-exome sequencing, and follow-up imaging were reviewed.
RESULTS: Imaging showed mixed destructive and sclerotic changes of the proximal tibia, fragmentation, marrow edema, physeal narrowing, periosteal reaction, and subsequent fractures with anterior cruciate ligament injury. Percutaneous biopsy was nonspecific. Despite reported localized knee pain and apparent responses to pinprick, temperature, and deep sensory stimulation during routine bedside examination, further history revealed lifelong hypohidrosis, heat intolerance, and heat-associated febrile episodes. Whole-exome sequencing identified two heterozygous NTRK1 variants, c.851-33 T>A (pathogenic) and c.2242C>T (p.Arg748Trp; variant of uncertain significance), supporting the clinical diagnosis of CIPA. Additional imaging demonstrated right navicular osteonecrosis. Brace immobilization, protected weight bearing, physical therapy, and family education were followed by fracture healing and improvement of genu valgum from approximately 8°-4°.
CONCLUSION: CIPA should remain a diagnostic consideration in children with unexplained destructive-appearing skeletal lesions, even when pain is reported. Discordant imaging, biopsy, and trauma history should prompt reassessment of autonomic features and consideration of genetic testing.

title: Extracellular Vesicle-Mediated Immune Reprogramming in Osteoarthritis: Modulation of the Gut-Immune-Bone Axis Through Immunometabolic Crosstalk.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is increasingly recognized as a heterogeneous whole-joint disease involving not only local structural degeneration but also systemic immune and metabolic dysregulation. Growing evidence suggests that dysregulation of the gut-immune-bone axis, which links intestinal homeostasis, immune responses, and osteochondral remodeling, may contribute to OA progression. Extracellular vesicles (EVs), released by both host cells and microorganisms, have emerged as important mediators of intercellular communication through the transfer of bioactive RNAs, proteins, lipids, and other functional cargos. In this review, we summarize current evidence for EV-mediated immune reprogramming in OA, with particular emphasis on immunometabolic crosstalk within the gut-immune-bone axis. We discuss how EVs from different cellular and microbial sources regulate macrophage metabolic plasticity, glycolysis, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, AMPK/mTOR-related signaling, adaptive immune responses, cartilage homeostasis, and subchondral bone remodeling. We also examine the potential involvement of gut-derived EVs in modulating intestinal and joint immune-metabolic responses. Although preclinical studies suggest that vesicle-associated signals may influence both intestinal and joint responses, direct in vivo evidence tracing endogenous gut-derived EVs to OA joint tissues remains limited. Finally, we review intra-articular and oral delivery strategies, EV engineering, biomaterial-assisted approaches, patient stratification, and major translational challenges. Overall, EV-mediated immunometabolic regulation provides a promising framework for understanding OA pathogenesis and highlights the translational potential of EVs as cell-free therapeutic platforms. Further mechanistic validation, standardized EV production, and well-designed clinical studies will be required to translate this potential into precision treatment strategies for OA.

title: Therapeutic potential of umbilical cord-derived MSCs in arthritis: Insights from preclinical and clinical studies.
abstract: Among different types of arthritis, osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remain the most common and primary cause of pain and disability worldwide, characterized by progressive joint degeneration and persistent inflammation. Although there have been developments in pharmacology, the available treatment program slows disease progression and provides only symptomatic relief. However, their ability to repair and restore damaged tissue is limited. This highlights the importance of regenerative therapy in actively modulating the immune system while stimulating tissue regeneration. We conducted a narrative review of PubMed, Scopus, Web of science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ChiCTR, focusing on preclinical and clinical studies of umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (UC-MSCs) therapy in OA and RA. Recently, UC-MSC have been emerging as a promising therapeutic approach due to their immunomodulatory and regenerative properties. Because they are harvested noninvasively, these cells have greater proliferative capacity and lower immunogenicity than MSCs derived from bone marrow or adipose tissue. UC-MSCs do not replace damaged cells; instead, they signal other cells to produce bioactive substances that reduce inflammation and promote cartilage repair. Data from emerging preclinical and clinical trials, which show significant improvements in WOMAC and VAS scores and a decrease in DAS28 with minimal adverse effects, suggest that UC-MSCs will improve pain and function and, in turn, overall quality of life. UC-MSCs represent a mechanistically distinct and clinically promising therapeutic effect for OA and RA, addressing both the inflammatory and degenerative condition of joint disease. However, there are still large, well-designed, standardized clinical trials that can best optimize doses and treatment plans. This narrative review summarizes the various forms of arthritis, disease pathogenesis, and preclinical and clinical evidence for the use of UC-MSCs in the treatment of arthritis, such as OA and RA.

title: Research Progress on Peripheral Physiological Responses and Central Neural Activity Characteristics of Competitive Anxiety.
abstract: Competitive anxiety is a core psychological factor constraining athletes' competitive performance. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on its peripheral physiological responses and central neural activity characteristics. At the peripheral level, the autonomic nervous system has been associated with a dual imbalance of sympathetic dominance and parasympathetic suppression. Nonlinear heart rate variability indices have been proposed to be more sensitive than linear indices in one small BMX study, but this remains preliminary and requires replication. Anticipatory cortisol elevation in the HPA axis has been interpreted within the inverted-U hypothesis, with high-trait-anxiety individuals showing delayed recovery dynamics in preliminary studies. Temporal characteristics of catecholamines in the SAM system may be more predictive of performance than absolute concentrations. Oxytocin and progesterone have been proposed as protective neuropeptide mechanisms, whereas sustained elevation of β-endorphin may mask fatigue perception and suppress immunity; these mechanisms remain largely hypothetical. Gut-brain axis research suggests anxiety-associated microbiota restructuring, and probiotic interventions have been associated with improved EEG activity and cognitive function in preliminary trials. At the central level, the Neurovisceral Integration model has been proposed as a framework for peripheral-central interactions. Prefrontal-limbic circuit dysfunction has been proposed to contribute to cognitive interference and somatosensory amplification. Frontoparietal attentional network imbalance may contribute to shortened quiet eye periods and impaired executive function. Cortical neural oscillations have been characterized by enhanced β-band activity with suppressed α/θ activity in some studies. Dysregulation of 5-HT/NE/DA neurotransmitter systems has been proposed to contribute to functional reorganization of the triple brain network through BDNF-mediated synaptic plasticity alterations; this remains a hypothetical integrative pathway. It should be emphasized that many findings derive from heterogeneous designs, small samples, and non-athlete or non-competitive populations; conclusions should therefore be regarded as hypothesis-generating. Future research should integrate wearable monitoring, ecological momentary assessment, and machine learning to develop individualized interventions based on neurobiological phenotypes, pending validation of the proposed biomarkers.

title: [Changing concepts and optimizing management models in geriatric orthopaedics in the era of population aging].
abstract: With accelerating population aging in China, geriatric orthopaedic conditions including osteoporotic fractures, joint degeneration and spinal degeneration are growing more prevalent. Centered on single-disease treatment and localized structural repair, the traditional diagnostic-therapeutic paradigm is no longer sufficient for clinical needs. Elderly orthopaedic patients frequently have multiple comorbidities and reduced functional reserve, with higher perioperative risks. Accordingly, treatment goals should shift from focusing merely on structural repair toward complication prevention, functional preservation and quality-of-life improvement. Experience in managing hip fractures, knee osteoarthritis and spinal degenerative diseases shows that comprehensive perioperative assessment, multidisciplinary collaboration, individualized surgical decision-making, early rehabilitation and secondary osteoporosis prevention are key to improving elderly patients' outcomes. In the future, geriatric orthopaedics should promote deeper integration of orthopaedics and geriatric medicine, build standardized care pathways and implement a full-cycle management system to realize a paradigm shift from "treating the disease" to "treating the patient"，from "structural repair " to " functional reconstruction"，and from "postoperative care" to "full-cycle management".

title: Fatigue-induced collagen denaturation alters tissue-level deformation.
abstract: Fatigue-induced collagen microdamage is thought to contribute to ligament and tendon degeneration and injury, yet it cannot currently be measured in vivo. Imaging-derived mechanical biomarkers could address this gap, but tissue-scale axial mechanical measures have shown limited sensitivity to early damage, and it remains unknown whether other components of tissue deformation track collagen damage as it accumulates during fatigue. To address this question, we repeatedly measured collagen denaturation and full-field tissue deformation in the same specimens throughout fatigue loading. Murine medial collateral ligaments were cyclically loaded for up to 2500 cycles, with collagen hybridizing peptide staining, confocal imaging, and deformable image registration performed at regular intervals. The resulting damage metric tracked established force-based indicators of fatigue, including hysteresis, peak displacement, and stiffness. Among tissue-scale measures, collagen denaturation was not associated with axial strain or apparent elastic modulus. In contrast, in-plane hydrostatic and transverse strain were associated with damage; hydrostatic strain was the strongest predictor of damage in rank-based analyses at both applied stretch levels. As denaturation accumulated, the lateral contraction accompanying tensile loading progressively diminished, indicating an altered apparent Poisson effect. These findings indicate that fatigue-induced collagen denaturation is reflected in multiaxial tissue deformation, and that strain perpendicular to the collagen fiber direction may provide a foundation for developing mechano-biomarkers capable of detecting early fatigue injury.

title: Editorial Commentary: High Tibial Osteotomy Is More Than Coronal Correction: Plan and Execute in 3 Dimensions.
abstract: Osteotomies around the knee are an excellent tool to treat unicompartmental osteoarthritis or support joint-preserving approaches and range from opening- and closing wedge high tibial osteotomy (HTO) or distal femoral osteotomy for coronal corrections to slope-reducing osteotomies for sagittal corrections and derotational osteotomies for axial corrections. HTO has traditionally focused on coronal plane deformity correction, yet growing evidence shows that medial opening-wedge HTO can introduce unintended changes in posterior tibial slope and axial tibial rotation. These multiplanar alterations may have important biomechanical and clinical consequences, particularly with respect to medial meniscus and anterior cruciate ligament loading. Although 3-dimensional preoperative planning and patient-specific instrumentation have improved the precision and reproducibility of coronal plane correction, the accurate execution of the planned correction in all 3 planes remains challenging. Intraoperative technical factors, including osteotomy hinge positioning, posterior cortical release, and differential gap opening, can influence sagittal and axial alignment regardless of the planning technique employed. A comprehensive understanding of 3-dimensional osteotomy mechanics is therefore essential to minimize iatrogenic deformity. Future advances in intraoperative navigation and real-time assessment of multiplanar alignment may improve correction accuracy and ultimately patient outcomes after HTO.

title: Temporal coupling shapes the effects of prolonged muscle-tendon vibration on sensorimotor EEG activity during motor imagery.
abstract: Motor imagery (MI) recruits sensorimotor networks overlapping those engaged during physical execution and represents a promising rehabilitation tool. While concurrent afferent stimulation enhances MI-related cortical engagement, the effects of prolonged proprioceptive conditioning prior to MI remain unexplored. This study investigated whether prolonged muscle-tendon vibration (MTV) could modulate cortical activity during subsequent MI, indexed by electroencephalographic alpha- and beta-band event-related desynchronization (ERD). Twenty healthy adults performed imagined maximal isometric knee extensions before and after 20-minute suprapatellar MTV (100 Hz) or SHAM vibration (30 Hz with foam interface) in counterbalanced sessions. Cortical engagement was assessed via EEG burst detection over central electrodes (C3, Cz, C4). Maximal force capacity, submaximal force estimation performance, and cortical responses during combined MI and MTV were also evaluated. MTV induced stronger vibratory responses than SHAM, consistent with enhanced proprioceptive afferent activation. Following MTV, voluntary force outcomes showed near-threshold changes consistent with the expected direction, namely reduced maximal force capacity and altered submaximal force calibration, suggesting modified proprioceptive feedback. MI performed after MTV conditioning exhibited reduced alpha- and beta-band ERD compared to SHAM, with greater vibratory-induced responses being associated with a less pronounced post-vibration beta ERD. Conversely, when MI was performed concurrently with MTV following conditioning, alpha-band ERD increased selectively in the MTV session, with no modulation in the beta band. These findings suggest that prolonged proprioceptive conditioning modulates MI-related cortical engagement differently depending on the sensorimotor context in which imagery is performed. Such state-dependent effects may support distinct intervention strategies aimed either at recalibrating maladaptive sensorimotor patterns or at enhancing cortical recruitment in rehabilitation contexts.

title: OA Chondrocyte-Derived Small Extracellular Vesicles Inhibit Migration and Chondrogenic Differentiation of CSPCs and Promote OA Processes by Releasing miR-199b-5p.
abstract: Cartilage-derived stem/progenitor cells (CSPCs) and chondrocytes play critical roles in osteoarthritis (OA) progression. Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) mediate intercellular crosstalk within the OA microenvironment, but their effects on CSPCs and underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study was therefore designed to investigate the regulatory mechanisms by which chondrocyte-derived sEVs modulate the chondrogenic differentiation of CSPCs. sEVs derived from chondrocytes isolated from healthy joint tissues (Normal-chondrocyte-sEVs) and OA patient joints (OA-chondrocyte-sEVs) were co-cultured with CSPCs. The impact of these sEVs on chondrogenic differentiation and CSPC migration was assessed using Alcian blue staining and Transwell assays. The regulatory roles of miR-199b-5p and sex determining region Y-box 6 (SOX6) in CSPC chondrogenic differentiation were further investigated using both gain-of-function and loss-of-function approaches. Compared with the Normal-chondrocyte-sEVs treatment group, CSPCs treated with OA-chondrocyte-sEVs exhibited significantly impaired chondrogenic differentiation and migratory capacities. Furthermore, we observed markedly higher expression of miR-199b-5p in OA-chondrocyte-sEVs compared with Normal-chondrocyte-sEVs. Mechanistically, OA-chondrocyte-sEVs mediated the impairment of chondrogenic differentiation in CSPCs through sEV-mediated transfer of miR-199b-5p, which subsequently targeted and suppressed SOX6 expression, thereby disrupting both the differentiation potential and activation status of CSPCs. This study demonstrates that OA chondrocyte-derived sEVs exacerbated OA progression through the miR-199b-5p/SOX6 regulatory axis. These findings collectively identify sEV-mediated CSPC dysfunction as a novel potential therapeutic target for OA intervention.

title: Understanding the Complexity of Athlete Sleep: A Systems Approach to Modelling the Athlete Sleep Environment.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athlete sleep can be disrupted by sport- and non-sport-related factors. However, the interactions of these sleep-related factors are not well understood. Systems science approaches, such as causal loop diagramming (CLD), provide an opportunity to map these interactions. This project aimed to (1) develop a CLD of the athlete sleep system describing the interacting variables, (2) identify feedback loops and potential leverage points to optimise athlete sleep, and (3) demonstrate the applicability of a CLD to guide the development of a sleep monitoring framework.
METHODS: A systems-based model of athlete sleep was developed using CLD, informed by existing literature and refined through a consensus process involving ten subject matter experts (nine from Australia, one from the USA). The model was then interrogated using network analysis to identify key variables based on their position and connectivity within the system. These findings informed the development of a generic sleep monitoring framework.
RESULTS: The CLD comprised 48 variables and 120 relationships across four domains: travel demands, behavioural and lifestyle factors, athlete condition and readiness, and resourcing and scheduling constraints. Overall, 12 key variables were identified, with hours of travel, number of time zones crossed, dose of caffeine, and amount of resources or expenditure available being the most connected upstream variables. Level of pre-sleep arousal, sleep opportunity, travel fatigue, and level of performance received the greatest number of incoming relationships, representing points at which multiple pathways converge. Physical condition, level of performance, quality of diet, and importance of competition most frequently linked different quadrants of the system. These variables informed a three-tier monitoring framework capturing upstream determinants and downstream consequences of sleep.
CONCLUSIONS: According to the CLD, sleep health in athletes extends beyond an individual behaviour issue and is influenced by the structure and functioning of sport systems. Interactions among travel demands, physical readiness, behavioural and lifestyle factors, and organisational constraints sustain athlete sleep health over time. Consequently, meaningful improvements in sleep health are likely to arise from both system-level interventions and individual behaviour change strategies.

title: Hybrid multimodal exercise training promotes enhanced recovery after surgery and improves musculoskeletal strength in patients with osteosarcopenic obesity: A clinical study protocol.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Osteosarcopenic obesity (OSO) is a progressive, systemic condition characterized by declines in skeletal muscle mass, strength, and function, accompanied by bone loss and adipose tissue accumulation, leading to adverse health outcomes including frailty, poor quality of life, high fracture risk, poor postoperative recovery, and mortality. It is more common in older adults, with physical inactivity and malnutrition being the main etiological factors, especially lack of exercise. Regular physical activity combined with appropriate dietary intervention is necessary to achieve optimal therapeutic effects for OSO. However, conventional exercise may be difficult for older adults with OSO who often present with frailty, and little is known about the role of exercise in promoting enhanced recovery after surgery and improving musculoskeletal strength in OSO patients. Hybrid multimodal exercise training, which involves targeted training based on an individual's physical and health status, may benefit bone, muscle, and quality of life. This clinical study investigates the feasibility and effectiveness of hybrid multimodal exercise training in promoting enhanced recovery after surgery and improving musculoskeletal strength in patients with osteosarcopenic obesity.
METHODS AND DESIGN: One hundred and twenty older adults diagnosed with OSO will be assigned to two groups: a hybrid multimodal exercise training group and a usual care group. Assessments will be conducted in the hospital, including baseline and post-intervention evaluations of health and function (body composition, bone mineral density, frailty score, balance ability, short physical performance battery, timed up-and-go test, activities of daily living). OSO patients will undergo a combined exercise intervention primarily based on resistance training in hospital and community settings for 12 months. Most older adults lack regular physical activity, leading to progressive muscle atrophy, impaired physical function, and substantially limited daily mobility. This initiates a vicious cycle wherein frailty, poor physical performance, sarcopenia, osteoporosis and adiposity reinforce each other, rendering structured exercise training extremely difficult for older adults. Unlike conventional combined training regimens that simply stack independent exercise modalities, this study implemented a hybrid multimodal exercise intervention. Hybrid multimodal exercise training (HMET) is a 12-month, supervised, progressive structured exercise intervention that systematically integrates resistance training, aerobic training, balance training, and flexibility training. It is designed to improve musculoskeletal strength, bone mineral density, body composition, and functional outcomes following enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) in patients with osteosarcopenic obesity (OSO). The four components are allocated within each training session according to a prespecified ratio, with periodic progression of training load to sustain adaptive responses.Characterized by low entry barriers, the intervention is easy for older adults to start, well-suited to daily life, and requires little specialized equipment. Patient functional status will be assessed using the Fatigue, Resistance, Ambulation, Illness and Loss of Weight Index (FRAIL), Tinetti Performance Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA), Timed Up and Go Test (TUG), Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), and Activities of Daily Living (ADL) scale. Body composition will be measured by multi-frequency bioelectrical impedance analysis. Bone quality will be assessed by measuring vertebral HU values using energy CT, and bone mineral density T-scores of the lumbar spine and femoral neck will be analyzed by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA).
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Our study protocol has been registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR), a primary registry of the WHO International Clinical Trial Registry Platform (ICTRP). Registration website: https://www.chictr.org.cn/. Registration number: ChiCTR2600116975. The study protocol and statistical analysis plan (SAP) are available on this website.

title: Therapeutic Potential of Plant-Derived Exosome-Like Nanovesicles in Musculoskeletal Disorders: Osteoporosis, Osteoarthritis, Bone Repair, and Skeletal Muscle Recovery.
abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders, including osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, impaired fracture healing, inflammatory bone loss, and sarcopenia, are major drivers of pain, frailty, falls, disability, and loss of independence in aging populations. Although current pharmacological interventions can inhibit bone resorption, relieve pain, or suppress inflammation, their clinical impact is often constrained by limited regenerative efficacy, suboptimal tissue targeting, long-term safety concerns, and insufficient capacity to address the multifactorial nature of chronic musculoskeletal disease. Plant-derived exosome-like nanovesicles (PELNVs), also referred to as plant-derived extracellular vesicles or exosome-like nanoparticles, have emerged as naturally organized lipid-bilayer nanoplatforms enriched in bioactive lipids, proteins, small RNAs, metabolites, and phytochemicals. These intrinsic features position PELNVs at the intersection of natural-product pharmacology, regenerative medicine, and nanoscale drug delivery. Accumulating evidence suggests that PELNVs derived from yam, ginseng, plum, Pueraria lobata, Morinda officinalis, Lycium barbarum, Drynaria roosii, watercress, grape skin, Chinese leek, and other edible or medicinal plants can modulate key processes involved in musculoskeletal homeostasis, including osteoblastogenesis, osteoclastogenesis, bone marrow mesenchymal stem-cell fate determination, chondrocyte senescence, mitochondrial quality control, inflammatory signaling, gut microbiota-derived metabolism, and skeletal muscle remodeling. In parallel, engineering approaches such as bone-targeting peptide conjugation, cartilage-binding peptide functionalization, chitosan-based shell assembly, hydrogel encapsulation, microneedle-assisted delivery, and localized depot systems are transforming PELNVs from crude vesicle preparations into programmable bio-organic therapeutic platforms. This review summarizes current evidence for the application of PELNVs in osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, bone and alveolar socket repair, inflammatory bone loss, muscle atrophy, sarcopenia, and exercise-related recovery, with particular emphasis on mechanistic insights, delivery strategies, translational challenges, and future standards for preclinical development. Oral bioavailability, causal cargo attribution, long-term safety, and manufacturing reproducibility remain unresolved.

title: Revisiting the Role of the Long Head of the Biceps in Shoulder Stability.
abstract: The long head of the biceps (LHB) tendon has traditionally been regarded as an expendable structure in shoulder surgery, often sacrificed without significant functional consequence. Histologic studies identify neural elements within the LHB and therefore provide biologic plausibility for afferent signaling; however, they do not establish an independent or clinically important contribution to proprioception. Cadaveric biomechanical studies demonstrate that applied LHB loading can resist humeral head translation, assist joint centering, and share load with capsulolabral structures under specific experimental conditions. Conversely, electromyographic and clinical studies show limited routine LHB recruitment during isolated shoulder motion and generally favorable outcomes after tenotomy or tenodesis. The evidence therefore supports a context-dependent model in which the LHB functions as a secondary stabilizer whose relevance varies with arm position, pathology, patient demands, and the integrity of surrounding structures. The LHB should be viewed as neither universally expendable nor universally essential, and surgical decisions should balance the dominant pain generator against the potential mechanical contribution of the tendon in the individual shoulder.
